All right. When I was 15 years old, I was homeless. And I never imagined I would ever be up here on this stage talking to you right now because I didn't think that far into my future. My priorities were getting enough money for bagels. And if I was extra lucky, whoops, can I go back? Cream cheese. My goal is to make me very hungry this morning. My clothes I found at donation centers, books, necklaces I made if I had to, spare changing and begging strangers on the street for money, and 25 cents made a huge difference in my life. If I had a dollar six, it meant I could have a hamburger at Burger King. That was a big deal. I slept under bridges and abandoned lots. I squatted unused sheds and attempted hitchhiking from Phoenix, Arizona to New York because why not? I heard it was amazing there, the land of opportunity. The streets were paved with gold. I didn't make it, but I made it as far as Hemes Springs, New Mexico, where I live in a commune digging ditches to earn my stay in the middle of winter. It looked a lot like this. You know, I don't have enough time to talk today about how I became homeless because I think there's just too much to go into there, the reasons why. But I think it's more important to talk about how I got out. And pretty much, you know, I've often wondered, and so have others, like how against pretty much all odds did I make it up here on this stage? If you don't know me, I'm Cy Advanisher. I'm a venture capitalist at Founders Fund. It's one of the top venture firms in the world. I've invested in companies in my career such as Uber, SpaceX, Postmates, Thumbtack, Carta, Niantic, right here, and more. It's difficult to give a short answer as to how I made it here, but if I were forced to say it would be these five things. I've tried to distill it down into these exact points. So let's start with incrementalism. A lot of people tend to think that incrementalism is a bad thing. But how do you go from nothing to something at all? It doesn't happen overnight. Suggesting it does, I think, is irresponsible, and it's out of touch with the realities that a lot of people face. I look at every day as a new day, every moment as a new moment, every conversation's an opportunity to learn more. Little by little, I improved, but I still didn't look far into the future. I look to the next day, to the evening. I set constant goals for myself, tiny achievements. When I was homeless, it was the bagel. It was getting a shower. It was my personal safety. It was getting better at all of those things. When I had a home and worked, it was about becoming better at every aspect of that job and striving to make more money constantly. The more money I was making was a reflection of the skills I picked up and the knowledge that I obtained. I turned everything into my life. Can we go back a slide? Sorry. I turned everything into my life in a game of leveling up. It's easy to judge that making life a game sounds gross, but it was a difference at one point for me between life and death. When I was 16, I became a ward of the state of Arizona. I was picked up by my favorite police officer, Officer Pratt. We'd become good friends. We were accustomed to these sorts of encounters by then. Usually I ended up in a group home, a detention center, or my mother would take me back for a short period of time, but this day was different. Officer Pratt took me to Dairy Queen. He got me some ice cream, then he took me to the courthouse where he got me a plate of spaghetti. He let me sit where the judge sits while I ate, and then after some time passed, I finished. A woman came in and told me she was my public defender. I had no idea what that meant. I wasn't sure why I needed to be defended from the public. It was kind of strange. But she explained that the judge was coming in, and so was my mother. My mother would stand on one side of the room when the judge spoke to me. I was to address him as, Your Honor. My only response to all of this was, Okay. It all happened so fast. The judge asked me some questions, and then the judge asked my mom if she wanted me anymore, and she said, No. She didn't look at me. The judge rambled some stuff, told me I was officially a ward of the state, to be released to my probation officer, my new parents. My new parents told me I had 48 hours to find a place to live, or I'd be placed in a girl's home. Having lived in those places before, I knew I never wanted to go back. I had to continue to go to school. I had to get a job. And I had to have a gallon of milk in my fridge. Yeah, that was a requirement. It's really strange. No lactose intolerance doesn't matter. To be grown up, you have to have milk. There were no boys in my house. I had to submit to random drug testing. And I had to be home by 9 p.m. every night. I'll never forget the smell of the air and the sun on my face as I walked out of the courtroom that day. I was free -ish. I never had to go back to my family. But I had 48 hours to figure out adulting. I didn't have a phone. I didn't have a home. I didn't have a car. Just the shoes and the clothes on my body. I didn't have a job. I had nothing. I sat on the corner and collected my thoughts and went through all of my options. I had one friend who was an adult who lived on her own. So I walked to her place. Luckily, she was home. She let me stay. And bonus? She told me she was moving out soon and I could have her place. Which meant I needed to get a real job. Up until this point, I had my hustle. Some under -the -table illegal jobs. My first job was slinging mashed potatoes at Fur's Cafeteria. It's a hot spot for elderly people touring Route 66 by Megabus. From that point on, just like the 48 -hour time limit, I treated each day as a game. In which I would try my hardest to level up on something. Anything. I set weird goals for myself. I didn't always win the game, but every day I would get up, I'd start over. I played games like figuring out how to make 25 cents more an hour. How to use a cash register. What all the skills were that I needed to become my boss anywhere that I worked. When I found I could no longer play the game where I was, I moved on. I worked elsewhere. I was obsessed with making more money. Because that was the measure of success in my game. The game's called capitalism. And it actually saved my life. So like a lot of young people who care about other people, I started out as a socialist. And I thought corporations were completely evil. And eventually I realized that corporations and capitalisms were the key to my freedom and ultimate success in this world. I started listening to the lyrics and the punk music that I jammed out to more. And I realized that everything that I actually believed was wrong. I moved to electronic music like you were listening to earlier. I tried to avoid words in my music while I tried to figure out what I believed. I eventually shed every bit of clothing with a brand. Anything associated with me with a tribe. I didn't want people to sum me up in one look. And I wanted to keep people guessing. Individualism. There was more to me. I started reading business books. I started my first business making and selling t -shirts. My life started improving for the first time. And I started dreaming about a future. A future in which I was a business person. It didn't really matter at that point what kind of business. I started to form my own identity. I was a person. I was cyan. I was capable of things. I had food in my fridge. I still had to put things back at the cash register. But I wasn't hungry all of the time. Individualism is I work on to this day. Because we aren't defined by labels or groups. We are multifaceted and a combination of a lot of things. I am not a woman. I am not a Democrat. I am not a Republican. We can all be part of a group. But we are always who we are. And we are all capable of independent thought. Mentorship and technology. You know, there were a lot of amazing people on my journey. They who taught me that I could be more than what I was. They didn't make me successful. But they told me that I could be. When I was homeless, I looked like one of those street kids you see on Upper Haight with the piercings. Patches and a dog, spare changing. I was what we might refer to now as a gutter punk or a crusty kid. I met one of my best friends to this day, walking down the street wearing something that I made. The feeling of seeing somebody wearing something you created is just not describable. You are a startup founder, as you probably know when you see your logo out there. I stopped this person, and we geeked out on making stuff, which led to an invitation to hang out and his phone number. We eventually did hang out, and he had something magical with him. A laptop. Up until this point, computers were something that were not for me. They were unobtainable. They were expensive. I would just break it. I had no use for one, but when I saw him sitting there in the cafe, in the dark, I knew I had every use for one. I could feel myself yearning for it, and I asked him, Can you get online with that? What else can you do? He showed me all of his art, the stuff he was coding at work, and he took me to a place where we could dial up together. The sound of that modem, and if you've never heard a modem in your life, I recommend that you listen to it, was like the wind on my face stepping out of that courtroom again. And before I knew it, I was on a thing called IRC, Internet Relay Chat, chatting with people all over the world. I was reading about things I was curious about, and I was absolutely hooked. I didn't want to do anything else. I suddenly knew my future, and it had something, anything, to do with that thing and the Internet. Chris exposed me to a world I never knew was possible. He brought me to my first DEF CON 23 years ago, which is a hacker conference. He introduced me to hacker culture, and suddenly my brain was fully engaged for the first time in my life. My friends encouraged me to get a tech job. I didn't know how, so they told me if I start at the very bottom, I could work my way up. I like this. It sounded like a new game I can play. So we decided on telephone tech support for dial -up. We role -played for a few days. This was the Windows 3.1 95 era, with the clouds on cyan -colored background. And when they were satisfied that I knew enough about TCPIP, DNS, trumpet, windsock, I set off to interview for a job. I landed my first tech support job working at a place called Extreme Internet. I was on cloud nine. I had a desk, a computer, a chair, a phone, and I had a pager. I was grown up. I thought I'd finally arrived. And for a short period of time, I became complacent. How could I possibly want anything more? I had a damn chair. So in between calls, I registered domain names. They were free then. And when they were no longer free, you could register them until the $100 bill came in the mail. And then, you know, it was yours for 90 days regardless. The co -founder of Extreme Internet, this is him, Lee Burton, came over and stood over me one day, and I looked up at him as he plopped a book on my desk. Thud. He took his fingers and he tapped on it. He said, You're far too smart to be sitting here registering domain names. You should read this instead. How do you know I'm registering domain names? Read the book. You'll figure it out. That was creepy. When he walked away, I tossed the book in the corner. Who the hell was he to tell me that? I wasn't going to read that stupid book. What's wrong with registering domains? Nothing. A few months later, I looked over at the book, which was collecting dust, and I cracked it open, and I read about 15 or so pages, and on one of the pages, it changed my life trajectory. It was a page about the power of root on a Unix operating system, and the book was called The Essential Guide to System Administration. On that page, it went through great details to explain that one should be super careful with root access, and went through the ways that people make common mistakes that allow people who shouldn't have access have it. The thing that stuck out to me was something called a shell escape. Basically, if run a script that executes a command as if it were root, you can escape out of the script when it's running and gain root access. I thought about all the scripts we used at Extreme Internet, and which one I should try it on. You know what? Password resets for our dial -up users. So I ran the script. I escaped out. Then I had to read the book more to figure out what to do next. I finally typed, Who am I? And the shell responded, Root. I jumped out of my chair. I couldn't believe it. I next figured out if I had the password, if I had a password, Root must have a password too. So, what do you do when you are in this situation? Well, you change the root password. So I did. I carefully wrote the password on a little piece of paper, hardly able to contain myself. I walked into my boss's office. I slammed the piece of paper down in front of him. What's that? He asked. Your new password, I said proudly. That book you gave me is amazing. He looked puzzled at me and said, Impossible. So I told him to try it. His old password didn't work. His new password did. After a walkthrough of how I did it, he said, You know what, Sian? Go grab a chair. Come sit with me. You're now a system administrator. He gave me a promotion. That day, I became his Padawan. In a lot of situations like this, I think people would be fired. Lee, on the other hand, saw what I was capable of, and he nurtured it. He taught me all about Linux, BSD, how the internet actually works, how to set up routers, DNS servers, email servers. He trained me for two years. I went from making $8 an hour to $15 an hour, which was a truly life -changing event. A lot of my friends who were in the tech industry in Arizona during this period of time started moving here to Silicon Valley. A friend of mine one day emailed me a link to Google and told me to try it out. And I saw the I'm feeling lucky button. I don't know if you guys remember that, but you would type in something and it would give you some random website. And maybe it had something to do with your search term. Maybe it didn't. It was then that I realized, because of this button, that everything magical I wanted to be a part of was here in San Francisco. I told Lee I had to leave. It was time for a new Padawan. He promoted and trained my friend Jessica, who now, because of his nudge and opportunity, is a software engineer. I threw everything in my car in 1999 and I moved here and I didn't have much of a plan. There was this guy I was seeing on Craigslist. That was my plan. The guy and I broke up, so then there was this Craigslist. I landed my first job and I went from $15 an hour to $35, which in San Francisco is probably about the same as what I was making in Arizona, as far as I get you for rent. I played the game some more, many jobs, learning how to code, foregoing a lot of friend time and late nights, until I finally broke six figures in 2003, because of Pat Peterson and Scott Weiss from Ironport. Scott Weiss was the CEO and one of the founders. He was the first person that I confessed to that not only did I not go to college, I was also a high school dropout. They both gave me promotions and enough stock over the years, they're based on my performance, that eventually once we sold to Cisco, years later, I had more money than I ever thought I would ever have in my life. So towards the end of my career at Ironport, I started dating and eventually married that guy. That's Scott Bannister. I had this windfall from my equity. I didn't know what to do with it. I turned to Scott for advice. Should I buy property? Stock market? He says, well, you can do what I do and put it into incredibly risky startups. Scott had identified that I was a super user, an early adopter of pretty much everything. He'd been angel investing for 10 years, and before I joined him, he noticed that I was using every product he was getting intros to months ahead of time. So he started asking me for advice about things like Twitter. But honestly, you couldn't ask for a better mentor than Scott. My first angel check went into SpaceX. I was terrified. But it was exciting. I was literally blowing up my money on launch pads. Money I'd slept under my desk making, years and years of working super hard into rocket ships. I became addicted. My husband and I figured out that our division of labor worked really well for us. I like giving talks like this and going to events and taking first meetings, and while he likes to sit on the couch, he's introverted, he prefers to work at home and meet very, very few people. And then there's this guy, Brian Singerman. He was on the board of a company that I started. He had just joined Founders Fund. He started off as an associate and is now a general partner at our fund. We'd often get together and make bets on companies, talk about the world of investing. One day, he invited me to get coffee with him. I thought it was just another one of those days. And then he said, how would you like to join Founders Fund? They had just closed their sixth fund and they needed another person and they needed to help expand the team. This is a question I thought I would never get. I was on the short list of people they thought would be a good fit. Brian told me at the table that my track record and the deals I've done qualified me for a role, a role I didn't think I would ever have, and that he believed that someday I'd be one of the greatest venture capitalists in the world. I'm still working on that. I still had to interview after days of interviewing. Here I am. And when I found out I landed the role, I felt that wind on my face again. I have a chance to play in a new arena and stretch myself intellectually. I'm always searching for the wind and somehow I'm here. Again, just about against all odds, I'm here and if you ask me how I did it, I can only tell you that I was endlessly curious. I surrounded myself with people smarter and more capable than me. I played the game every day. I still do. And nobody was around to pat my back. I learned how to give myself props and believe in myself. Also, can tell you that mentorship isn't something that needs to be formal. Lee knew he was mentoring me, but some of the most profound things that happened to me were not formal arrangements. For example, at TC40 in a room, this is the first Disrupt, it was very small, Mike Arrington put me on stage because he found that I had something important to say. He was the first person who believed in me. Or Jason Kalkanis, for one time I was getting on stage, stopped me just before I got on stage and he said, you know, knock them dead. You earned this. You can do this. You can help people without spending much time at all. It's all about how you approach life and who you give opportunities to. If in a position to do so, and face it, every single person in this room is in the position to give someone help and advice and to tell someone, great work. You can do this. We can be our own worst enemies. I made my own luck by simply waking up every morning and telling myself I could do anything. By getting out there and meeting people and simply showing up, I created opportunities. And sometimes, I failed miserably. But we don't get perfect scores in any game we play. We stomp around, we scream our fists at the sky, we take a deep breath, and then once again, we press start. Thank you.

[SPEAKER_00]
Hey everyone. In this video I'm going to be talking about some of the characteristics that VCs are looking for in founders that they talk to while pitching their startup. The kind of four key things that people are looking for are really come down to systems level thinking, domain expertise, technical insight based on that domain expertise, and drive. So with systems thinking what I mean by that is being able to look at a market industry technology stack and look at the factors involved and kind of connect the dots between factors in a way that lets you project forward how are things going to change going to evolve over time. So clearly that ties into the concept of domain expertise. If you've got systems level thinking applied to an area you just by kind of building up your understanding of each of those concepts each of those technologies each of those factors and connecting those dots inherently going to have a stronger deeper understanding of the market that you're heading into as a founder. And so those two are kind of tied together. Of course not everyone's brain lends itself to that systems level thinking automatically looking at a bunch of factors and connecting the dots between them. So how do you demonstrate domain expertise the kind that VCs want when you're pitching your startup? This is where drive comes in. People talk loosely about wanting to work with founders who are passionate who are driven to build a company but really early on if you're talking angel investment seed round you know any of those early checks where you haven't really built a business to evaluate thoroughly you really only have to go off of your evaluation of the founder. so you know how do you compare one founder to another? Oftentimes that what it comes down to is is this person passion enough if they're not from this space originally to have done the homework done the legwork of investigating the factors involved in that market that they think they're gonna be able to build something really valuable in. So this is where kind of combining drive with knowing that systems level thinking is important is kind of a way to manually if that's what's required build out that domain expertise. Literally build out for yourself definitions of important terms, notes on important factors and how they seem to be changing to what extent you understand future roadmaps that are going to be important again if you're talking about components. Having that kind of understanding of the different factors at play is how you get to the last characteristic that I mentioned. That's technical insight. And so technical insight sounds like something that again only a technical founder who's been deeply immersed in the underlying core technologies involved in a market would really be able to wrap their heads around. But I'm using kind of a broader definition of technical insight. This is something that you'd see in for instance the book How Google Works. What you're really talking about are understanding the rules by which a game is played and that might actually mean why does this technology work this way, what technical trade -offs were made and based on new emerging tech or new techniques that have been discovered in academic research labs or what have you. know perhaps it really comes down to oh well actually if we built this component this way or if we use this new kind of component this new experience is possible technical insight very well might mean something along those lines. But if you're using that broader definition of technical insights it might be something that say a salesperson would pick up on. Oh customers within this segment tend to care about this factor. You know to an extent that's that wouldn't seem obvious to someone who's just building from first principles a solution that would address their needs. When you're in the context of a VC pitch some of those things might seem obvious especially if you're talking to someone who's you know built a company in that space themselves. But you know it's important to speak to your experiences what you know that no one else knows. If you can give that those examples of things that you've found over the course of your time being immersed in those workflows and how your passion drove you to ask questions that went beyond the surface level observations to go well what might it mean if we pulled on that thread a little bit. You know that that's really how you get to this combination of the four characteristics I'm talking about. If you're driven you're compelled to look at a domain deeply. You're going to take a systems level approach to mapping it out looking at the factors that matter and by doing that you almost can't help but identify technical insights that will let you build a differentiated product solution within that space. And even if you're not a technical founder yourself by having a perspective that is unique you can still find ways that you know obviously can deliver value that no other company whether it's an incumbent or startup is delivering on and that's how you can get a VC really excited.

They just do it earlier in the day. You might work up a little extra early and do your yoga and do your running. You might stay up a little later and do that. You might get a gym membership, but you go to the gym at 1 o 'clock at night. So everybody handles it differently. Me, myself, I have a guilty pleasure. And my guilty pleasure is comic books. So you know, I would carve out some time during my day where I'm going spend 10 -15 minutes and just enjoy a comic book and not be bothered. know. And you try to find, you know, little short times here or there. If your thing is movies, you might try to find a time where, you know, you might pick a day like Saturday was my day where I took care of laundry. I kind of slept in a bit. I relaxed a bit. You know, so I gave myself a few hours of, you know, the stress time before I went back to work. So you might want to pick a day. You know, if you're a movie person, you know, it might be Saturday. On Saturdays, I'm going go to the movie. I'm going to watch a movie. You know, I'm going to watch a movie, stream one on my computer, lay in the bed, not be bothered, you know. Find some sort of normalcy, something that, you know, you like to do, keep up with it. You if you have a favorite TV show that you watch every week, watch it. You you might not be able to watch it when it comes on, but find some time during the week to watch it. I'm a huge football fan. You I'm a Baltimore Ravens fan. I'm a Baltimore guy. So on Sundays when football came on, I was watching the Ravens game. was me and Norma was streaming on my laptop. Now, I might have another program open, you know, writing up some strategy or go over your notes for the week or preparing for a meeting with my team to go over how the last week went. But it was on. It was there. If I wanted to take, you know, 10, 15 minutes and just stare at the screen and watch it, I took that, you know. When you go to an accelerator, they ask you to work as closely to 24 -7 as possible. But we all know that's not possible. You need some of that time to yourself.

[SPEAKER_00]
So I'm thinking that if you're going to allocate time to not only your guilty pleasure, but just really giving yourself some down time and to kind of relax a bit from all that high up -tempo 24 -7 kind of work, do you ever come into conflict with the people that you're working with, like your team members, saying, like, you're putting too much in your guilty pleasure or your relaxation while they're, like, how do you, I guess that was just a random question in my head. Like, someone might be working that full 24 -7 and feel as if you're not putting in the same effort as them.

[SPEAKER_01]
I don't know because I've been through two accelerators now. And in both instances, for myself, my team, and all the other teams, everybody had moments where they kind of, you know, you had a little bit time to yourself. But for the most part, throughout the day, everybody was working hard. So if you took 15, 20 minutes to take a break, or if you left on a Saturday and went to the mall and hung out for a little bit, or if instead of working in the office, you wanted to go to a coffee shop, and while you're at the coffee shop, you wanted to have some down time, maybe read a book for a little bit. Nobody, nobody had any issues with that because we were all feeling the same kind of stress. We were all feeling the same kind of pressure. And we all had other responsibilities to friends and families and loved ones. So everybody kind of understood that, no, we can't work 24 -7, but you work as closely. And if there were moments when me and my team were working hard and we were a collective, and we were all sitting around the table together, you know, plotting or something, know, whiteboarding something, at those points and times, no, you were all in. Everybody was all in. But if you were whiteboarding and it's been, you know, eight hours, and within that eight hours, you got some code done, you got some documentation done, you got some testing, you're still doing more whiteboarding, if you stop for a moment like, hey, you know, I'm going to be back, guys. I'm going to go down the street to the restaurant and I'm going to buy myself dinner. And just sit at the bar and have dinner at the bar by yourself, have a drink, eat dinner, and come back. People were generally okay with those kind of things. You know, everybody's going through it, so everybody's pretty understanding. And it also depends on the makeup of your team. You know, my team, you know, my two teammates were two of my best friends.

[None]
So we

[SPEAKER_01]
understood, you know. My one co -founder, when we went to San Francisco to the New Me Accelerator, he got married a month before we left. So, you know, when he was out there, it might be one o 'clock in the morning, he's been working all day, coding all day, and his wife calls. Now, if he wants to take his laptop and go into another room where he can talk to his wife while he's doing some work, we didn't have an issue with that. Now, when he got out of, you know, the other room and he was done talking to his wife, we might ask him, so what should you get done? But for the most part, like, everybody kind of understood.

[SPEAKER_00]
I remember that you said that your first accelerator was in Baltimore, but your second accelerator was in San Francisco.

[SPEAKER_01]
Right.

[SPEAKER_00]
So did you visit San Francisco before you even went to the accelerator?

[SPEAKER_01]
No. My first day ever in San Francisco was the first day of the program.

[SPEAKER_00]
And how was that?

[SPEAKER_01]
That was interesting. I showed up and I went to the house. So for that program, they already had a housing for us set up. I went to the house, kind of moved my stuff in, kind of met with everybody, and then they showed us where the office was. We went to the office and had our first little bit of orientation. And learning about San Francisco and the city kind of came later, but I still didn't take full advantage of it because I was so busy working. Like, I was there on a mission. I wasn't there to see San Francisco. I was there to work.

[SPEAKER_00]
But it came to you during, like, the second month, though, right?

[SPEAKER_01]
Around the second month, you started to get into the groove of things. Like, you started to fill out your schedule so you could see where you could have downtime or where you could do things. And I also started having more meetings outside of the office. So, you know, I might meet with an investor or an advisor at a restaurant downtown that I've never been to and a part of San Francisco I've never been to. Or I might meet with another entrepreneur who's local to that area, and they wanted to hang out and go grab a drink. Well, you know, that would be my opportunity to kind of see a little bit around the city and get to see what else was going on. Like I said, Saturdays was my day, so there might be one or two nights where on a Saturday night, I decided to go to a bar and, you know, maybe just hang out for a little bit. You know, me and a couple of the other people from the cohort decided to go out together. And that's another thing. know, by the second month, you've now been working with these people for, you know, several weeks. And you start to develop relationships and friendships among the other teams. You know, people who you hang out with, people you connect with, people you start to spend time with because they're the people you're spending most of your time with. It's your co -founders and other members in the cohort. And so it kind of becomes almost like a family unit. It's almost like being in college. Like you're in college, but you're confined to this one small class. So it's like 20 or 30 of you, and that's the whole college. And so you spend all your time together. Everybody's taking different classes and working on different things, but you see each other all day, every day. And those relationships help, you know, having other people around you who understand your struggle, who understand the process that you're going through, the hard questions that you're trying to answer, having them to bounce things off of, it's extremely helpful.

[SPEAKER_00]
So I'm trying to find a way in terms of understanding the second month. So the second month is just continuously working and putting in those hours, and then also finding that balance and then just naturally developing that sense of family with everyone that's in the accelerator. Is there anything else that we should be aware of in terms of the second month?

[SPEAKER_01]
So the second month is definitely, you know, continuous working. And the second month is very pivotal for how you're going to end the program. So the second month, once you get to the midway point of the program, you need to have a really clear idea of where you plan to be at the end of the program. Because the purpose is at the end of the program, you're going have your demo day when you pitch to investors. So you want to make sure you set yourself up in the best position possible to make that pitch. So you want to have your product and your idea and your business model completely solid. And during this process, you know, you've had six or seven weeks to meet with a lot of smart people and get a lot of advice and get to understand your market a whole lot better than you did before you got there. And if you start to feel a little issue with your business model or with your product and you start to have that feeling in the back of your head like, hmm, maybe I should pivot, you maybe we should change our direction, that's the time to do it. You know, if you start to feel that, do it sooner rather than later. Because that's about the last time where you'll have a chance to do that. If you make a pivot at the six -week mark, you still now have six weeks of dedicated time to make that pivot happen and maybe try to get it out into the market and see if you can get a little bit of traction, some numbers behind it, just so you have something to show come demo day. What you don't want to do is when you have three weeks left of the program, you're like, all right, we're going to make the change. But you get the demo day and you're not ready. You don't have anything to show. So around that midway point is where you kind of want to be like, okay, this is where our product is, this is where we are, this is how solid we are. You know, this is our identity and this is what we're going to do moving forward. You really want to have a clear -cut, you know, idea of what you're doing. Because when I said when you first come in month one, you want to have a plan on what you want to do and over a period of time how you want to do it. Once you get there, you've now gone through six weeks plus of learning and going through your plan and that plan started to change. It's fluctuated. Different priorities have popped up. And now at that six -week mark, midway mark, you should have a better understanding of what, you should have a very clear understanding of what your last six weeks are going to be like. know, that plan for the last five or six weeks should be very, very clear at that point. You should, you know, you should be able to pinpoint a lot of stuff on that. And you need to be solid on that. If you're not and you're still kind of going with the flow or still trying to figure out what you're going to do with your product, you have a lot of work ahead of you and not a whole lot of time. Because once you get to the end of the second month, you start to feel that time crunch. You start to realize, oh my goodness, I only have four weeks before demo day.

[None]
And

[SPEAKER_01]
when you think about that, the last week to week and a half is all you getting ready for your pitch. You're not doing as much work. As a CEO who I was pitching, you're not doing as much work and much planning or strategizing as you were. So really, once you get to that point, you only have maybe two or three weeks left of actually working on your product and getting everything together before you start switching gears and focusing all your energy into being ready to pitch your product.

[SPEAKER_00]
So you told us what exactly what to do. But what's your personal experience? Because I know that you had a personal experience in terms of this pivoting.

[SPEAKER_01]
My personal experience was around the midway point when I was in San Francisco. We came up with an idea and we found out it was really unique. And I kind of had the idea pivoting in the back of my head, but I didn't pursue it. I didn't pursue it until after we had gone through the program. And that was one of my biggest regrets. Because I never got to show all those investors who were there on demo day what our pivot was and what the power of it was. And that became a sense of concern for me. That was something I wish I could take back. So this is my advice to you. If you feel that and you want to pivot, do it sooner. There was actually another company in our program who went through the same issue. And what happened for them was they wanted to pivot. They kind of saw it. They didn't do it. But waited until after the program. And they'll tell you. They wish they had pivot sooner. And that might have been the reason why their company didn't make it. Same for us. The fact that we didn't pivot and pitch that on demo day might have been the reason why our company didn't make

[None]
it.

[SPEAKER_00]
So that was your second

[None]
month.

[SPEAKER_01]
That was my second month. Awesome. So I guess that wraps up with what the second month of an accelerator is like. Next week, Kate and I will be back here to do another one. And we're going to talk about the third and final month and the dreaded demo day.

[None]
The

[SPEAKER_00]
demo day. That's awesome.

[None]
So

[SPEAKER_01]
it's been good, everybody. And we'll see you next week. Bye, everyone.

[SPEAKER_00]
Bye, guys.

[SPEAKER_02]
Hi everyone, this is Roach from Life's Dermastery and today I'm excited to have Charlie O'Donnell, who spent 20 years in venture capital, first as an analyst at Union Square Ventures and he opened the first Round Capital's New York office and then founded Brooklyn Bridge Ventures, where he has than 100 startups including companies like Hungry Root and Bridget and now he coaches VCs, teaches at New York University and just wrote the number one bestseller, is Founder Unfriendly, What Investors Won't Tell You About Getting Funded. Welcome, Rishaw Charlie. Thanks for having me. Awesome, you know, before we talk about your book, I'm really interested to know, you know, how did you get your journey in this crazy world of venture capital and startups?

[SPEAKER_00]
So I started out at a place that a lot of people don't start out and don't really think about and that is I started out on the limited partner side. So when you are pitching a VC, you don't really think about the fact that this person has also had to pitch to get money.

[None]
I'll do it every

[SPEAKER_00]
two to four years, not every 12 months, but so the VCs are funded by large institutions like pension funds, endowments, family offices, foundations. And I worked for the General Motors pension fund. It was one of the largest corporate pension funds in the world and had been investing in venture since 1978, well before my time. But they were invested in all of the top brand name firms that you can think of. And so VCs used to come in and pitch me as well as private equity funds, distressed and mezzanine debt funds. So I came from the institutional side and in 2004, I took a pitch from Union Square Ventures. And it was when Brad Burnham and Fred Wilson first started the fund. The idea of doing a New York based fund in 2004 was not an obvious one. Most of the venture capital in the US had been the Bay Area, a little bit of Boston, but New York really was not a big venture capital community. But I really, really took a liking to them, thought they had sort of a very different approach.

[None]
And

[SPEAKER_00]
Fred and I had started sort of a back channel conversation. Fred started his very famous AVC blog in November of 2003. I started my blog, thisisgoingtobig.com, about three months later in February of 2004. So I've been writing for about 22 years pretty consistently. And it was a way for us to really get to know each other and for them to get to know how I thought. And so one day after GM passed on their fund, which was a huge mistake because obviously that has been a monster returning fund. I tried to pound the table, but they decided it was too small. I just emailed Fred and I said, what does a junior venture capital investor even do? Like what do I need to get there? Do I need an MBA? Do I need a computer science degree? Yeah, science And if you ever emailed Fred you're lucky you get one line back. And he just wrote, you want to come and find out? And that was it. That was the whole conversation. That was the beginning of my being in a venture fund, you know, kind of career. and we went to lunch after and I decided to join. So I was the first analyst at Union Square. A couple of years later, I went over to help First Round Capital, which is known for backing Uber and Looker and Flatiron Health, helped them open up their New York office in 2009. And after a couple of years there, broke out on my own to start Brooklyn Bridge Ventures and went solo as a solo GP.

[SPEAKER_02]
No, very interesting. A big fan of Fred Wilson and Brad Feld. I was fortunate to have Brad on the show. You mentioned earlier that mediocre startups get funded while Brilliant One gets passed over repeatedly. So is there any specific pattern that you're seeing play out whether worse company wins that check, maybe because of a better deck?

[SPEAKER_00]
Yeah, it's interesting. So it's very hard to compare two companies. Right. So there are ideas that are better than others, but they are run by people who may not be able to prove that they have the same ability to execute. Right. And so when you're you're talking about sort of winning over a venture capitalist or any investor, really, there's a lot of components to it. And, you know, for for starters, there has to be a match between your intentions and the venture capitalists need for return. So, for example, you may decide you have a a really great app idea and you want to launch it for a particular community within the local market in India, let's say. Yeah. And let's say that market is fairly small there, although nothing is very small there. But but the real opportunity is in other countries for any number of reasons. You have to make it clear to a venture capitalist that it is your intention to do a global rollout to get the kind of numbers that you're talking about. If your whole pitch is about what you have done up until this point and you're trying to prove to someone, you know, we're a really great team. Look at what we did with very little. Look at how we bootstrap this. Look at how we're breaking even. And the whole entire pitch is is backward looking because you're conscious of. Do I even deserve to be in this meeting? Let me prove to them that I'm legit by telling them about my past history. This person is buying tickets to the future. That's what they want to hear about. They want 80 percent of the pitch to say, tell me how this returns my fund. So so your app could be better. You could be a better developer. But the VC isn't going to fill in the gaps that you left. Right. And so if you're not telling that you're you have an intention to build a much bigger business, then they're going to be like, you know, that's that's that's a shame because I really like that product. But I just don't feel like that founder is ambitious enough.

[None]
And

[SPEAKER_00]
they're making that based on what they heard in the pitch. Other times it's about relationships and reputation. Right. So, for example, you look at somebody like Mark Laurie, who sold Quincy, which was diapers dot com, sold jet to Wal -Mart. And the first thing he ever did, which was a baseball card site, he sold to Topps, the baseball card company, for a couple of million dollars or something like that. Literally, the guy has exited every single thing he's ever done.

[SPEAKER_01]
Yeah.

[SPEAKER_00]
And no one would say that any of those ideas on the face are like game changingly brilliant that no one ever thought about before. He is just a world class executor with a track record of being able to sell whatever it is that he builds. So there are a lot of people who might sit there and say, you know, is 50 million dollar seed round or whatever you call the first thing that he raised for for Jad or Wonder, which is his business now. My idea is better than that. Maybe. Right. But you are not de -risked in the same way. You don't have the same reputation. And I think one thing that founders miss out on is they they're dismissive of that. And they don't sit across the table and be like, yeah, you know, like clearly this investor doesn't know me from a hole in the wall. They have no ability to diligence my ability to execute on stuff. So so before I say that, you know, giving a founder like that 50 million dollars is crazy, I should walk into this meeting saying, OK, my challenge is proving my ability to execute. And I know that going in because this is the first time that I've done this before. And this is an execution based business. And it's hard not to be dismissive in the face of getting really excited about an idea.

[SPEAKER_02]
You made an interesting point. Like, I think second time or third time founders do do get a preferential treatment. But especially in the age of year, you've seen a lot of younger founders also get funded where they're I mean, it's a it's a new playbook, you know, where they're saying that he is eating into SaaS. What are your thoughts? Does it make sense to have that same sort of SaaS playbook or, you know, like a CEO would have the same sort of playbook or a founder would have the same sort of a playbook? And is it still relevant now?

[SPEAKER_00]
You know, there was a really good article put out by Euclid Partners recently about how like the average age at YC is getting younger. And when Paul Graham first started, he had made a comment that I don't know if he actually picked an age, but I he sort of alluded to the fact that like late 20s was sort of a sweet spot because you had sort of gone out and gotten some experience. Right. But you were young enough to not be jaded or to be using the latest tools or whatever his reasons were for backing younger founders. And now it's becoming even, you know, sort of younger than that. Listen, I think there are some very special founders across all ages that are able to get out of their own way in terms of what they lack or the the hindrances they have because of their age. And I will say that for both 20 year olds and 55 year olds. Right. And, you know, so I think that like your challenge kind of remains the same because there is there is bias across every meeting. Right. And so if I go in as a 20 year old and I go pitch, you know, some VC who led enterprise sales for some big, you know, Decacorn company and that's their background. And and they're historically thinking you have to be well networked and all of this sort of stuff. I should go in there. Having done the homework of saying we've talked to a lot of enterprise buyers. We have these design partners and they have told us that here's their challenge. Right. So you can go in as a 20 year old who's never had a full time job and speak very eloquently and in a prepared way about how buyers in your market buy. And the history of things that people have tried to sell them that doesn't work. Right. In the same vein, you could go in as a 55 year old founder who has all the networking connections in the world. And unintentionally walk right into the biases that somebody might have about you by, for example, sending someone a PowerPoint. And it just when somebody does that. Right. And they are older. I was like, listen, we're all humans. We all have a bias. If you're not sending me a Docsend or Notion, whatever, you are falling right into the trap of my main concern that you have an old school way of doing something. Right. And so you just want to be conscious of don't give people extra reasons to turn you down. Right. And so if you're you're 20, don't be dismissive that you just think that, you know, the ed tech buyer is not going to be concerned about security or anything else like that. And if you're, you know, you know, the older founder, don't be dismissive of the fact that, you know, your competitor has raised all sorts of money and they're a bunch of 20 year olds or whatever, because they might be learning faster than you are now. And that's important.

[SPEAKER_02]
Yeah, no, absolutely. I completely agree on that. And and you you you also analyze pitch decks. Is there one slide or a couple of sites in in a deck which you think should not be there for the founder and you would want to tear it out?

[SPEAKER_00]
Yeah. So first of all, I think you have to be very careful when you are following any kind of template whatsoever, because your story is relatively, relatively unique. And so here's the way I think about story. First of all, VCs have no attention span whatsoever. If any VC is listening to this podcast, they probably already started doing their email. Right. And that's what you're fighting against. You're fighting against the attention span of a three year old, basically. And so you always want to start with your your strongest hook in the beginning and keep the momentum up. Keep the energy up. Keep the interest. Keep them leaning in. You want practice on that. to talk to a student class who is 100 percent on Zoom because they are going to be completely checked out if you are not, you know, constantly hitting every single slide with excitement and and reasons to lean in. Right. Every company is different. Right. For one company, it might be the team that did incredible things in their last startup. For another company, it might be the fact that you are selling into small city governments and you cold emailed 500 of them and 80 of them have already closed on your product just from that one initial cold email. You pitch something like that. And VCE is going to be like, wait a second. You just like you're selling into governments and you sent you. You have like an 18 percent close rate on just one cold email. Like how did how did you do that? I need to understand, you know, how you're doing that. And you need to keep that momentum up. So I think what you really have in any kind of pitch deck is is three things. So you have team, you have market and you have traction. Now, people might have thought I was going to say product, but VCs, I think, are actually quite bad at evaluating what a good product is. One, because they're not the customer. Right. So they may not necessarily know what features are going to win. Right. So traction is a proxy for the product working. They want to see somebody using it. And team, to be honest, team is a really high bar. Right. So if you have previously sold something and made people money, that's the top tier of team. You will probably get another shot at doing that again. Second tier is like uniquely qualified to do this thing. When I was at First Round Capital, I backed a founder to do some marketing software for bars and restaurants and small businesses. He had previously run sales at Seamless, which merged with Grubhub here in New York for 10 years. Like literally, he could write a book about selling into pizzerias and bars. Right. That's how he was uniquely qualified to do that thing. The tier after that is just smart people working hard. And that is a big, indistinguishable tier. Right. Like you may love your co -founder, but you have to admit they are a VP at HSBC in their previous life, which means that they know something about FinTech. Right. But I in New York City, I could throw a rock and hit somebody else who's at VP level at a bank. Right. That's not unique. So you say great team is like, is this a must back team? Right. With market, market is not just market size. Right. Market is, is there pull in this market for something? Are these customers looking for something new? Is the wind going to be, you know, kind of at your back? Or is this going to be, you know, skepticism? You look at the travel market, for example. Travel is very hard. There have been big wins at travel. know, Fora is doing quite well. Airbnb, obviously. Kayak. But there are headwinds that you have to be very conscious of. There's cyclicality in travel. There are established players. It's very hard to do paid customer acquisition in travel. Right. So there's all sorts of things you've got to be conscious of, despite the fact that it is a huge, huge market and people spend a lot of money on it. And traction. Not all traction is equal. There are some things where I would say are easier to do than others. You could be a great growth hacker and solicit 100,000 emails for your demo page. And you could say, hey, you know, we have all these people interested in the product. But maybe nine other similar products have been built before this. And like a dating app. Right. You could generate through field marketing and through growth hacking a lot of interest in your app. But making a good app that people will accept and why people choose one versus the other is really hard. Right. And consumers are picky. You need really great product design. It needs to be fast. You need sort of liquidity in that market. Right. There's enough people for you to go search through. The execution on that is really meaningful, which is why most VCs will not back a consumer product before it launches. Unless it is, you know, a previously multi -time back founder. But they just want to see, like, did you nail this product? Most times you kind of get two out of the three.

[None]
Right.

[SPEAKER_00]
Right market. We haven't done anything yet. Or we've done some stuff. It's an interesting market. Don't worry about who we are. Whatever the two things you get, that's what you're putting up front to kind of keep the momentum up.

[SPEAKER_02]
No, absolutely. This is like a master class in, you know, VC. But you were working at, you know, Brooklyn Bridge Ventures. And you made a last investment in 2023 across, you know, 105 companies. And it was focused on, 40 % was on female founders, you know. So how much of that portfolio composition was part of the thesis versus, you know, being accessible to, you know, those sort of founders who are, you know, female founded or, you know, female founders or, you know, had a unique or different background.

[SPEAKER_00]
So it's a really great question. And the answer is zero. It's not a thesis at all. And I have thought a lot about access to capital because that number is very different. is statistically significant compared to a lot of other funds. So when I would answer that question, I'd talk to reporters or what have you, they'd say, there's no conceivable way you didn't intentionally do this because the number is so much higher than what you see elsewhere. And there's a couple of things that go into that. First of all, I was a first check VC. And so if you're not a first check VC, you are most likely just backing who has been backed. Right. So it's very hard to knock a series A VC for not backing enough female founders because they're probably only backing people who already have raised the seed round. Right. And so it starts very early. So as a first check VC, you're just backing the entire universe of people who are looking for capital so that that is easier not to succumb to whatever the sort of percentages are in the market. The second thing is that I think how I approached a lot of pitch meetings was different. So there are lots of instances where, in my experience, not to generalize, men and women have different approaches to projections and different levels of comfortability with projections. In 2020, I launched Rare Breed Ventures as a response to the lack of access to capital for founders of color and founders outside of major investment hubs, as well as a response to the lack of cultural competency from many VCs when it came to investing in founders who didn't look like them or didn't come from similar backgrounds. The current rules limit the amount of capital and sources of capital for small and new investment funds, leading to less capital to help drive innovation, economic growth, and drive creation, especially when we're talking about companies started by founders of color because we know that in particular, black -led funds are four times more likely to invest in black -led companies. Also keeping in mind that almost all of the black -led venture funds in America would fit under the new rules of the ICANN Act because most of us have funds that are less than $150 million. With the ICANN Act, such limiting factors would be greatly reduced, allowing more accredited investors to have opportunities to participate in the asset class. With lower minimums, investors can potentially invest smaller amounts of money into more VC funds to spread out their risk and better diversify their investments. [SPEAKER_00]
So you invest in founders. You're a people first company. What do you look for in someone who fits the rare breed, you know, ideal?

[SPEAKER_01]
Every company and every founder is its own unique situation. But I'm looking for one from a business standpoint. I'm looking for people who have a very unique and direct opinion of how they do customer acquisition, experience and retention. If you show me you know how to find customers, you can get them to buy your product and they can keep coming back, then you might have a chance to actually win. And by having that mindset, allows me to take out my own biases where I don't have to know exactly what market you're in. If I know that you find customers, they love it and keep buying it. They love it and they keep coming back to buy it. Well, that's how we become the firm that never misses out on the opportunity to invest in a company like Spanx. Right. You can imagine, you know, when Spanx is first pitching to a bunch of VCs like there are a bunch of folks who don't get it. But the moment she says, well, you know, I go to these department stores and sell it to women. Women love it. And most women are going to buy four of these a year. OK, I don't need to know everything about this. You clearly figured out a market that something is working. And then, you know, sometimes it's the intangible. So like the woman I mentioned who I backed in Baltimore, I was working with her for like three years and nobody wanted to invest in her. And so what she did was she became a surrogate mother. She gave birth to twins to raise the money to start building her prototype. Like, you can't tell me that's a person who won't do whatever it takes to make to be successful. You know, like that level of grit, most people will never be able to see. And then on the flip side, I invested in a 17 year old kid out of Baltimore who basically hacked Venmo to get his first 25,000 customers. One of the smartest people I've ever met in my life. I just made a bet on him because he was one of the smartest people I've met. Right. So every found in every situation is different. But it's those unique things about them that kind of set them over the edge. We just committed to a company the other day where we're talking to the founders, a really cool company. And I know it's on LinkedIn that he ran this nonprofit helping returning citizens or people who are returning out of jail. And I asked him about it. He's like, yeah, you know, my dad was a lawyer and he was a pioneer in justice reform. And he's like, you know, really helping people and supporting people is really important to me. And that's why I'm like, oh, yeah, yeah, you're definitely the kind of person we want to invest in. So it's those things that sometimes go beyond just the business that we look for.

[SPEAKER_00]
And these are these are people that the traditional venture capitalists would have never discovered because they're not in Baltimore. They're not in your community. They're not interacting with these people. And you're going to events to meet these people, correct?

[SPEAKER_01]
Absolutely. I mean, before we had a global pandemic, I spent a lot of time in my community and other communities. You know, I spent a lot of time in Birmingham, Alabama and St. Louis and Detroit where you get to meet these folks. get to go in these communities. You go you go speak at a Chamber of Commerce event. You go speak at Urban League event. You go hang out at the Lesbians Who Tech local meetups. I can't tell you how much crap I got when I used to work for the investment on the state of Maryland for going to the Lesbians Who Tech meetup. They're like, why are you going to this event? I was like, it says Who Tech? Like, I'm looking for tech entrepreneurs. Like, I might find one there.

[None]
You don't discriminate.

[SPEAKER_00]
Equal opportunity here.

[SPEAKER_01]
That's such a novel concept, right? And so I just learned that when you go wow and you're intentional, you get access to far more people and far more entrepreneurs than you do just waiting for them to come to you.

[SPEAKER_00]
Yeah, well, you talked about the 17 -year -old kid, right, that sent people a penny on Venmo to bring them to ScholarMe.com. That's pretty interesting. What ended up happening to that 17 -year -old?

[SPEAKER_01]
So that 17 -year -old Femi ended up getting some money from us at the state of Maryland. Used that to go live in New York and raise $500,000 from a bunch of ex -Goldman Sachs folks. Ended up going to Y Combinator, which is the premier startup program in the country. Raised $2.5 million coming out of that. Got some money directly from the founder and got led by a large venture firm. And now has a company that is growing by leaps and bounds and will have some major updates coming out soon.
