They’ve got the level of trust, they’ve got the buy-in, and then you can do the… Maybe it’s not the CGM model where it’s buy one, get one, but you break it down a further level and say, “What is accessible?” Well, doing finger pricks like the same way that barber shops are currently doing. It’s a very interesting model to say these are micro steps that we’re taking to create more visibility into this mission, this education.
McKeever Conwell (40:18):
Absolutely. And the way you framed it, what if Levels partnered with Squire? That could be incredible. I’m not saying that’s something that has to happen or we’re saying it’s going to happen or anything, but the idea of you take a company that’s so community based and connect it with a company that’s health based, that have becomes a really powerful tool for changing lives essentially. And there’s probably hundreds of other potential partnerships or things that could happen where just introducing people to metabolic health. And then taking the next step of like, “Okay, now you’ve been introduced to it, here’s how you can improve it, here’s how you can monitor it. Oh, here’s a device that you could use that could be significantly impactful in monitoring it.” That becomes really powerful.
Ben Grynol (41:15):
Let’s talk about this last aspect that, again, it comes down to there’s disparity, but there’s also ways of creating more access and opportunity from a talent perspective. What can we do? What can companies do in general to create more opportunities for underrepresented communities?
McKeever Conwell (41:44):
Be more intentional and deliberate by allowing these communities access to open jobs. Open jobs and then also resources on how they can be trained or get to the point where they could do those jobs. You don’t need to spend four years in college to work in the HR department. You don’t need to spend four years in college to be a social media expert. You don’t need to spend four years in college to be a compliance expert. You don’t need to spend four years in college to be a software engineer, that’s what you’ve learned from all the boot camps. Imagine if you take the… Because in every city they have these organizations that help train up those in the community with different hard skills and soft skills. What if you work with those communities, like say, “Hey, we have a need for these type of engineers or these type of positions. Here’s some resources. We would love you to add this to your coursework.”
McKeever Conwell (42:51):
Be more hands off as an organization, as a company, because you still got to grow, you got to do what you do. Allow people from different means and different economic backgrounds to now have the opportunity to gain a skill and get a job at a pre-IPO company. Getting a job at a pre-IPO company literally helps families create generational wealth. But typically the only way you learn about those types of jobs is if you’re already in the circles or you’ve already worked at one of these companies before or you have a friend who works in one of these companies. We have companies in our portfolio where their first hires of color came from my personal network. Well, the only reason those individuals got a chance to even know to apply to those companies is because I told them to. These companies just putting out their job boards, which typically go through their investor network or their social media network, never gets to the communities that I come from. Because the communities I come from, going back to what we talked about earlier, don’t socialize the idea of working at these companies.
McKeever Conwell (44:02):
We hear Facebook and Google. We don’t hear about Level Health or Main Street or Rebundle or any of the companies in our portfolio that are doing incredible work that I know plenty of people who are more than qualified to work at, but they just have their corporate day jobs or they don’t have access or the potential to own stock or own equity in the businesses they’re working for. So all they have is their 401k. Being an employee at Levels pre-IPO, you’re going to get some stock options along with a great salary, along with post-IPO you get to say, “Hey, I was one of the first X amount employees at this company. I watched it grow from a hundred employees to a thousand employees, and I’m happy to help another company get there.” That puts you in a completely different stratosphere as you go and progress in your career. And so one is making sure that those opportunities are shared far more broadly, whether it’s through folks like me or having even liaisons whose job that’s just what their job is to do.
McKeever Conwell (45:06):
And then also sharing resources with those community activists and evangelist and educators to say, “Hey, share these resources with your communities, help them learn these skills. This is the next wave. We’re not going to have all the construction jobs and administrative jobs going forward. And even if you going to have administrative jobs, what an executive administrator was 10 years ago, looks vastly different today. Here are the things and skills they need to know.” It’s not about knowing Excel, they need to know Salesforce. They need to know Workday. Now you need to work on PeopleSoft. Let’s help the community get there.
Ben Grynol (45:52):
Yeah. I think it’s a matter of the nod. Sometimes people just need the reassurance to be like, “Yeah, you can do this too.” As you said, it’s like people know of, they know of Facebook or know of Google or know of… If somebody’s into tech, they might know of Main Street. They might know of these companies that are earlier and not as prominent. But they need the nod to be like, “Yeah, you can do this too.” Is there anything stopping you? Go apply. Kind of like you got the nod from your friend that was like it was a nod in the sense of, “Yeah, do it. Just do it. There’s literally nothing stopping you.” And you’re like, as soon as you ask yourself, you’re like, “I guess, yeah, there really isn’t anything stopping me.” So it’s the nod and the reassurance that gives people the nudge in the right direction.
Ben Grynol (46:45):
And it’s one of those things that with that cue, that starts to spread because, as you said, somebody goes and they work at a company that they go from they’re in the first 20 employees and the company goes to of 500 and they saw all of these different growth paths. And then they can go and they can help other people. And they become the model to help other people learn and say, “Yeah, you can do it too.” It’s such a important foundation that we can’t miss. The other important thing that’s happening from a societal perspective is the outlook on remote work. Somebody can be outside the valley, but let’s drill down even further, so there’s all of these different tiers. So we’ve got the tier one cities like the New Yorks and the, we’ll call it the bay area, we’ve got all that maybe lean into tech a little bit more. And then we start to get Buffalo and Baltimore and Philly, we get all of these other cities and you can drill down one more layer. What’s stopping somebody in East St. Louis from being a knowledge worker? Literally zero.
Ben Grynol (47:52):
But the challenge becomes the nod. The challenge becomes they need, and the reason I use East St. Louis is one of my friends is from there originally, and he lives in Atlanta now, but when he goes back, he’s kind of the guy that everyone’s like, “Well, I can’t be that guy.” And he tells all his friends and he’s like, “There’s no reason you can’t, there’s literally no reason you can’t. Just because I don’t live here anymore doesn’t mean I’m any different. We all grew up together.” And so he’s trying to spread that message to his friends that you can do anything you want. And now removing geography as a constraint makes such an impact, and it’s a matter of spreading a message within communities from the ground up so that it can get further and wider.
McKeever Conwell (48:44):
Yeah. It completely changes the paradigms and things, especially it used to be, “Hey, I have access to the opportunities within hour drive of my house.” Anything beyond that, I can’t do. So now as remote work becomes more prominent, now I have access to any job in the country that I can do from my home or I can do from a virtual office. That completely democratizes access for work and the type of work. It used to be, yes, if you’re a startup, we want you to start your company in San Francisco because this is where the concentration of talent is. This is where concentration of money is. This is where concentration of talent is. It’s no longer true. This is where concentration of money is, but talent can be dispersed. And you can find the best talent anywhere. I find an amazing coder at Idaho, he can code all night long from Idaho.
McKeever Conwell (49:43):
I don’t care as long as he’s getting done the work we need done. And then we have the ability to get on a Zoom call and be able to interact. And then maybe once a quarter will fly him out to the office and so we can actually have some face time and grow as a team. That changes the idea of talent. That also changes the idea for startups and companies where they start, not having to move. If you start in your local community but you realize the talent that you’re looking for isn’t local, if you have a hard time getting people to move to you, you no longer have to pick up and move to where the talent is. You can be like, “Okay, look, if you don’t want to live where we are in East St. Louis, that’s okay. You can stay wherever it is that you are, and we can still get this work done.” That’s something that we weren’t able to do before and now we’re able to do it in mass. So I’m excited for the future.
Ben Grynol (50:35):
You got a new painting back there since last time we talked.
McKeever Conwell (50:44):
I do.
Ben Grynol (50:44):
I think it’s nice.
McKeever Conwell (50:47):
It’s from a local Baltimore artist.
Ben Grynol (50:49):
Nice, very cool, very cool.
McKeever Conwell (50:51):
Everything Baltimore around here.
Ben Grynol (50:53):
Yeah, dude.

Feb 10, 2022, 2:58 PM ET·20VC with Harry Stebbings·6 min
Mac the VC Answers a Quick Fire Round of Questions with host Harry Stebbings | 20VC
Mac the VC, Harry Stebbings, McKeever "Mac the VC" Conwell II
Rare Breed venture capitalist discussed the personal and professional challenges of balancing family life with the long-term demands of multi-fund operations during an appearance at the Harvard Club. The speaker advocated for increased diversity in venture capital and urged greater flexibility toward founders requesting non-disclosure agreements, while highlighting Unspun as a recent investment that leverages 3D printing to create zero-waste jeans. The conversation also emphasized the importance of founder conviction in deal-making and concluded with a call to return to pre-pandemic social norms through a public health message.
Feb 4, 2022, 11:01 PM ET·20VC with Harry Stebbings·43 min
Mac the VC on the Journey from Homeless To Becoming A VC | Full Interview with Harry Stebbings
Mac the VC, Harry Stebbings, McKeever "Mac the VC" Conwell II
Mac, a former software engineer and two-time founder, launched Rare Breed in 2020 after raising $10 million through a public solicitation model that bypasses traditional general partner commitments and leverages rolling closes. The Baltimore-based firm targets pre-seed companies outside major tech hubs, prioritizing returns among underrepresented founders in the Americas and the UK rather than adhering to industry gatekeeping norms. By utilizing a flexible capital call structure and public marketing under Regulation 506(c), Rare Breed has established a non-traditional investment vehicle designed to democratize access for emerging managers and overlooked talent.

Interview with Mac Conwell, Founder and Managing Partner, Rarebreed Ventures
By The Kenyan Wall Street
- October 26, 2023
- October 26, 2023
Global NewsStartupsTechnologyVenture Capital
Share
Founded in 2020, Rarebreed Ventures is a Pre-seed to Seed venture fund consistently on the hunt for rare breed entrepreneurs. This pre-seed fund invests in exceptional founders primarily outside of large tech ecosystems, earlier than everyone else.
The firm writes cheques of up to $250,000 as the first or one of the first investors in exceptional startups and is based in Baltimore, Maryland-USA.
“When I established Rarebreed, I was not thinking of making any international deals and thought this could be done, perhaps, later. I had a lot of people asking when we were going to invest in Africa. It so happened that the last investment we did out of fund 1 was out of a company that is based in Uganda.” says Mac Conwell, founder and managing partner at Rarebreed Ventures.
Our team spoke to Mac Conwell during the recently held Kauffman Fellowship Summit in Nairobi.
“We are also keen on the agriculture space, which occupies a huge portion of Kenya’s economy. So we intend to begin looking for agro-based startups here in Kenya” said Conwell.

Let's Start Up Issue 6 | If it's not a hell yes, it's a 🙅🏻‍♀️
POV: You're a founder building a startup
Janine Sickmeyer
Nov 20, 2020
4
Share
Hi there 👋 Welcome to the Let's Start Up newsletter, curated by me, Janine Sickmeyer, a tech founder turned angel investor. Follow me as I share startup tips, industry news, founders you should know, and investors putting their money where their mouth is. Let’s Start Up, is a community of its own with an emphasis on the overlooked and underrepresented.
What's In This Issue 🗞
A brief look into what you'll be reading about.
Setting boundaries and saying no
Women and immigrant founders in the news
Two founders making moves in the world of CPG and anti-dieting
What's On My Mind 💭
I’ve been thinking…
In the world we live in today, it seems as though we are all accessible. We carry our phones with us everywhere we go, we sit in front of a computer and do video meetings with people more than we see actual humans in the wild. And because of these things, it's hard to turn off and hard to say no. Yes, being a startup founder or budding entrepreneur means that you're adaptable, driven, and hardworking. But that doesn't mean you should ignore your own personal limitations and boundaries.
When you're in the early stages, you want to take every opportunity that comes your way but let's be honest, sometimes the things you say no to actually provide you with a great opportunity - the chance to rest. This week alone I said no to several opportunities and turned down multiple mentorship and advisory calls. It's not because I don't want to help people or share my insights; it's because I need my own time and that's okay.
I am here to say that you don't NEED to have a reason to say no. We appear to be accessible at all times because of the internet but the reality is that no one has access to us 100% of the time and we are free to say no, turn down meetings, and not attend a zoom birthday gathering just because we simply don't want to. And setting boundaries with loved ones and family members right now are especially important. Of course, we all want to see each other but for the greater good of the country, it's more important to have a family un-gathering. We can still be grateful for one another while apart.
Let's talk about how to set personal boundaries during a pandemic.
First things first, I heard once that if it's not a "hell yes, it's a no". That seems appropriate right now.
If someone asks you to be on their podcast or speak at an event and you're not up for it, you should recommend a Black person to take your place. This is your chance to be an ally.
Remember that it's OK to decline business from a potential client or paid opportunity too. You don't have to say yes to everyone. And you don't owe anyone a reason.
The family wants to visit and you're uncomfortable having anyone over? Tell them that. They will be upset at first because they miss you but it's better for everyone that you don't sacrifice health for someone else's feelings.
As we head into the weekend, remember to set your own personal boundaries.
What I’ve Been Working On 💁🏻‍♀️
Things I care about that I want to share
Founder's Gift Guide
The holidays are coming up soon! Even though the holidays look a little different this year, we can still celebrate. I'm putting together a gift guide just for entrepreneurs. Who better to ask for gift ideas than fellow startup founders? Send me your favorite gadgets, products, and anything else you love that would make a perfect holiday gift. Look out for the post in the coming weeks.
Stagger's New Look
Stagger, one of my portfolio companies, relaunched their new website, and blog this week! The new-look identifies the purpose behind their product: helping brands tell their stories through compelling design. And, the graphics and animation on the site are stunning. Take a look around Stagger's new website and see how their app gives you the tools to tell your company's story effectively.
Ink-Paper-Publish
As I shared in the last issue, I'm writing a book about my startup journey as a solo woman founder. I'll be honest, writing a book is hard work and it's different than anything I've ever done before. I started working with Danielle Anderson, a book coach, earlier this year for guidance during the entire process - from ideation, the book proposal, manuscript review, and so much more. Visit Danielle's website if you want to become a published author! https://inkpaperpublish.com/
Recently Hit the Stands 📰
Things in the news I think you should check out
It’s crazy, but I started my own bank
Anne Boden, founder, and CEO of Starling decided to create a bank because of her frustration with modern finance and Britain’s broken banking system. Anne Boden is breaking stereotypes with her app-based bank that has won Best British Bank and several other awards. She reimagined banking in the male-dominated industries of finance, technology, and startups. Read more about her incredible story and how she grew Starling Bank to 1.8m customer accounts and a staff of more than 1,000 (with 40% of women in the senior roles).
The Double Standard of Female CEOs Moving Fast and Breaking Things
There's a problem that we need to address. Women CEOs are criticized for their mistakes more than their male counterparts. Over the last few years, there have been a number of women in leadership positions were forced to resign and apologize after making a risky move. Charlie O'Donnell shares the harsh reality women founders and leaders face, and how toxic work environments and news coverage are making matters worse.
The Real Reason Your Startup May Be Struggling
Founders have ninja-like skills. They're able to manage about a hundred challenges at once and grow their startup from the ground up. But sometimes the challenges that arise are caused by the founder themself. The problem many founders are having? Lack of communication with their co-founder. The good news is, you can break the cycle and set your startup on the right path for success with great communication skills with advice from Reboot.
Kansas welcomed my immigrant parents. Then I built Dropbox, an $8 billion company
Arash Ferdowsi, the son of Iranian immigrants, co-founded Dropbox in 2007. Since then, the tech company has grown to over 600 million users and $1.7 billion in revenue. His parents moved to Kansas City in search of more opportunities, and they were welcomed by their community. In this article, Arash shares his background and the importance of giving immigrants the support they need to flourish and innovate our world.
A Little Birdie Told Me 🐦
Tweet of the week.
Minal Hasan@minal_hasan
VC as an industry would be so much better if we as VCs acknowledged that we will never understand the business as well as the entrepreneur does and barring a few exceptions, we ain’t that bright.
12:41 AM · Nov 15, 2020
84 Reposts · 923 Likes
Hot Take of the Week 🔥
Somebody had to say it
Typical VC@typicalVC
when covid ends there’s a 100% chance we get travel agencies disguised as startups called shit like "flite" or "trāvl"
4:02 PM · Nov 13, 2020
55 Reposts · 774 Likes
Walk the Walk 💰
Investors putting their money where their mouth is.
Seven Seven Six invests in Founder well-being
Alexis Ohanian's venture capital firm support startups and the people who run them. He says that founders are the investment, and we couldn't agree more. Seven Seven Six sets aside 2% of what they invest in founders exclusively for health, well-being, development, and caretaking. Congratulations to Seven Seven Six for setting a new standard 👏
Backstage Capital's Impact
Since 2015, Arlan Hamilton's investment firm Backstage Capital has been giving underrepresented founders access to funding. The last five years were full of intentional and groundbreaking investing for Backstage Capital and they released their 5-year report to highlight the "past, present, and future" of the firm and diversity in venture capital. In this report, Backstage shows the hard data behind their investments and what other investors and companies are doing to make an impact.
African fintech startup Chipper Cash raises $30M
Ugandan Ham Serunjogi and Ghanaian Maijid Moujaled founded Chipper Cash in 2018, which allows person to person mobile payments in seven African countries without a fee. This fintech startup just raised $30 million in Series B funding, which was led by Ribbit Capital and Bezos Expeditions. Chipper Cash is adding even more features, like a Bitcoin marketplace and the option to invest in U.S. startups.
Founders You Should Follow 👀
Meet these founders who are making moves.
Jelena Jansson, Chunkie
Jelena Jansson founded Chunkie, an app that acts as a body confidence companion, to help people stop crash dieting. The app isn't for dieting, instead, it offers guidance on building a "better relationship with food, body, & mind." No restrictive dieting is involved, but there is a lot of support and encouragement from peers and mentors. Jelena is creating a safe platform to help us get BEYOND the scale, and this is the app we didn't know that we needed!
Andrea Hernández, Snaxshot
Product oracle at vibes.capital and forecaster Andrea Hernández started Snaxshot to provide insights and a market breakdown for the food and beverage industry. In each email, Snaxshots outlines upcoming trends and opportunities and challenges that companies in the industry might face. Andrea Hernández "sees for you" so you don't have to sift through the saturation and noise. We love this novel idea from Andrea and her eye for aesthetics. Subscribe to the Snaxshot substack (say that 10 times fast) here: https://snaxshot.substack.com/
What Founders Need to Know 🤔
Founder tip! Sponsor a niche newsletter
Take your marketing outside of the box by sponsoring a niche newsletter. Mac Conwell says this growth hack can help you reach customers more effectively and cheaper than google ads.
Are you using Notion yet?
Notion has changed the way my team and I work. It's like Trello, Google Sheets, Word, and more all in one. Founders, you need this.
Don't self sabatoge
When you're starting a company, it's easy to overcommit to engagements, become a little too adaptable, and get caught up in being a perfectionist. But this might be causing you to burn out.
Bitcoin for beginners
On Wednesday, Bitcoin prices saw record-high numbers. Check out this thread from Amanda Goetz to see how you can get in on this hot investment opportunity.
Startup Bookshelf 📚
What our community is reading this week.
A Promised Land by Barack Obama
Just this week, Barack Obama released his memoir, A Promised Land. He thoughtfully shares how he went from finding his purpose of becoming the president of the United States. A Promised Land details the first term of his presidency, which involved many landmark decisions and transformations. As the 44th and first African American president, Barack Obama reflects on the challenges and success he experienced while being on the world stage. I already started this memoir and can't put it down.
Before you go 🚪
Check out what you might have missed
Twitter now has stories, and users can't tell if they like the new feature. To fleet or not fleet?
The Wall Street Journal announced its list of women to watch in venture capital.
Tea can be a healing tool. Big Black Tea is helping the world heal and recover with a warm cup of tea.
BuzzFeed is acquiring the Huffington Post, uniting two digital media giants.
Thanks for reading! I’ll catch you next time. And don’t forget to share Let’s Start Up with your community!

McConnell's spinetail (Synallaxis macconnelli) is a species of bird in the Furnariinae subfamily of the ovenbird family Furnariidae.[2] It is found in Brazil, French Guiana, Guyana, Suriname, and Venezuela.[3]
Taxonomy and systematics
[edit]
Well into the twentieth century McConnell's spinetail was treated as conspecific with Cabanis's spinetail (S. cabanisi).[4] Since its recognition as a species its further taxonomy is unsettled. The International Ornithological Committee recognizes two subspecies, the nominate S. m. macconnelli (Chubb, 1919) and S. m. obscurior (Todd, 1948).[2] BirdLife International's Handbook of the Birds of the World adds a third, S. m. yavii.[5][6] The Clements taxonomy treats it as monotypic, with no subspecies.[7]
Genetic data published in 2011 supported that McConnell's spinetail, the dusky spinetail (S. moesta), and Cabanis's spinetail (S. cabanisi) form a monophyletic group. However, data published in 2013 has evidence that the dusky spinetail might instead be more closely related to the rufous-capped spinetail (S. ruficapilla).[4][8][9][10]
The specific epithet of McConnell's spinetail is misspelled with "mac" instead of "mc"; the species was named for a F. V. McConnell. By the rules of the International Code of Zoological Nomenclature the error is retained.[4]
This article follows the two-subspecies model.
Description
[edit]
McConnell's spinetail is 15 to 17 cm (5.9 to 6.7 in) long and weighs 18 to 20 g (0.63 to 0.71 oz). It is one of the darker of the Synallaxis spinetails. The sexes have the same plumage. Adults of the nominate subspecies have a thin pale line behind the eye on an otherwise grayish face. Their crown and nape are dark rufous; their back, rump and upperail coverts are dark olive-brown. Their wings are mostly rufous-chestnut with fuscous brown tips on the flight feathers. Their tail is dark chestnut; it is graduated and the feathers have pointed tips. Their chin and throat feathers are blackish with grayish white edges. Their underparts are mostly brownish gray with a slightly paler belly and a faint brown tinge on the flanks. Their iris is chestnut, their bill black, and their legs and feet olive. Juveniles are slightly paler overall than adults, with a gray and white barred throat and a browner breast and belly. Subspecies S. m. obscurior is overall darker and grayer than the nominate.[11][12]
Distribution and habitat
[edit]
McConnell's spinetail has a disjunct distribution. The nominate subspecies is found on the tepuis of southern Venezuela, far western Guyana, and extrene northwestern Brazil. Subspecies S. m. obscurior is found in the lowlands of Suriname, French Guiana, and northeastern Brazil.[2][7][3] The species inhabits the edges of montane and lowland evergreen forest, secondary forest, and in French Guiana some riparian forest. It favors dense undergrowth. In the tepui region it occurs at elevations between 1,000 and 1,900 m (3,300 and 6,200 ft); in the east it is mostly found from near sea level to about 1,000 m (3,300 ft).[11][12]
Behavior
[edit]
Movement
[edit]
McConnell's spinetail is a year-round resident throughout its range.[11]
Feeding
[edit]
The diet and foraging behavior of McConnell's spinetail are not well known. It is thought to feed on arthropods that it gleans from foliage and small branches, staying about 1 to 2 m (3 to 7 ft) above the ground. It is usually seen in pairs.[11][12]
Breeding
[edit]
The nest of McConnell's spinetail is a ball of sticks with an entrance tube on the side, typically placed in a shrub about 3 to 4 m (10 to 13 ft) above the ground. Nothing else is known about the species' breeding biology.[11]
Songs and calls
Listen to McConnell's spinetail on xeno-canto
Vocalization
[edit]
The song of McConnell's spinetail is a "dry rattle, ending in a higher pitched, full-stop 'drrrrrh-Tic' ". Its call is a "short, dry rattle, like 'drrrr' ".[12]
Status
[edit]
The IUCN has assessed McConnell's spinetail as being of Least Concern. It has a fairly large range; its population size is not known but is believed to be stable. No immediate threats have been identified.[1] It is considered fairly common but local. "Evidently a true forest species which, unlike many Synallaxis spinetails, does not occur in heavily cut-over areas."[11]

Descripción de PreMoney 2021 - The new faces of venture capital: Mac Conwell
On December 2, 2021, 500 Global convened the global venture capital community in Miami to its PreMoney 2021 conference for an interactive experience at the nexus of culture, technology, investment and global finance.
Mac Conwell joined us on a panel of emerging VCs. He founded Baltimore-based RareBreed Ventures a little more than a year ago to invest in pre-seed and seed founders outside of the major tech hubs.
On our podcast Rise of the Next, Mac tells us how he raised his fund the most unconventional way–by using Twitter. The social media platform enabled him to build a network in the VC community and learn about the world of venture capital.
His advice to underrepresented founders: don’t get mad, get even. Listen to his journey and more.

done anything. We wanted to take

now."

LBO Binge Crazes Congress 
Capitol Hill lawmakers are planning to put Wall 
Street's love affair with leveraged buyouts under the mic- 
roscope during the upcoming Congress, a move that could 
radically change broadcast merger financial strategies 
and revive legislative efforts to reinstate anti -trafficking 
rules. 
In the wake of this week's mam- 
moth $25 billion buyout of RJR /Na- 
bisco, House Telecommunications 
and Finance Subcommittee Chair- 
man Edward Markey (D-MA) has 
vowed to take a hard look at the 
junk bond -fueled LBO binge. 
"I'm enormously concerned that 
the amount of debt corporate 
America is running up is going to 
have a devastating effect on the 
economy when the inevitable re- 
cession arrives," Markey told In- 
vestment Dealers' Digest, a Wall 
Street trade publication. 
Markey's subcommittee also has 
jurisdiction over the broadcasting 
industry, and in 1987 it held hear- 
ings on reinstating anti -trafficking 
rules to curb radio station mergers 
and acquisitions activity. At the

RAB Manhunt 
Winding Down 
A special search committee charged with finding a re- 
placement for outgoing Radio Advertising Bureau Presi- 
dent William Stakelin has narrowed its search to a handful 
of candidates whose qualifications will be considered at a 
special meeting in about two weeks. 
"It's been boiled down to five 
names," Search Committee Chair- 
man Richard Chapin told R&R. 
"We're going to have a meeting on 
December 19 in Cincinnati atGreat 
American Broadcasting headquar- 
ters. All of our committee mem- 
bers are planning to be present." 
Chapin, a media broker with 
R.C. Crisler & Co., said about two 
dozen applicants have been screen- 
ed by the group. He confirmed that 
Wayne Cornils, currently Exec. VP 
and number -two man at RAB, 
would be interviewed for the post, 
but he refused to disclose the iden- 
tities of other candidates making 
the final cut. 
"We think we've got some very 
viable candidates in the group, 
most any of whom would do a good 
job if we can work it out," Chapin 
said. "There is nobody at the pre- 
sent time who has been mention- 
ed as the outstanding candidate 
and who would stand before any- 
one else." 
The search committee is com- 
posed of Chapin; Emmis Broad- 
casting CEO Jeff Smulyan; Dean 
Sorenson of Sorenson Broadcasting 
Corp. ; Mike LaRue of UA Com- 
munications; Nationwide Com- 
munications VP /Radio Steve 
Berger; and Buckley Broadcasting 
President Rick Buckley Jr. Chapin 
said Great American Broadcasting 
President Carl Wagner, the incom- 
ing RAB Chairman, would also 
participate in the December 19 ses- 
sion. 
Sources close to the committee 
told R&R that others on the list of 
prospects include Joe Dorton, the 
former CEO of Dorton Broadcast- 
ing; RAB Communications VP 
Danny F lamberg; New Yorker 
Robert Mounty, a former NBC Ra- 
dio executive who now heads 
Mounty Communications Inc.; and 
Warren Potash, a retired Capital 
Cities /ABC radio executive who 
operated WBAP & KSCS /Ft. 
Worth- Dallas. 
"Those are some of the names," 
said Berger, who added that "three 
or four" other candidates are un- 
der consideration. "I really don't 
want to release any of the names 
because I think that can only 
hinder the search. I think it would 
be wrong of us not to consider lots 
of folks, and we are still in that 
weeding -out process." 
Lyman Not Candidate 
The identities of possible can- 
didates have been the subject of in- 
tense industry speculation in re- 
cent weeks, with veteran RKO Ra- 
dio executive Jerry Lyman being 
named frequently as the top con- 
tender. 
"Jerry Lyman has not been a 
candidate," said Chapin. "He's a 
very able guy and I have a lot of re- 
spect for him, but I received no ap- 
plication nor did I have any conver- 
sation with Jerry regarding the 
job. It was only a media hype that 
he was a candidate, and I think it 
was an injustice to him." 
Chapin also denied that Olympia 
Broadcasting CEO Ivan Braiker 
and sales consultant Norm Gold- 
smith were under consideration, 
saying the two had never applied 
for the job. He declined comment 
on reports thatArbitron VPRhody 
Bosley and Communications Equi- 
ty Associates media broker Tim 
Menowsky had been dropped from 
consideration. 
ers that he was concerned that 
many stations were cutting corners 
on public service in order to serv- 
ice huge debt loads. 
Earlier this year, Infinity Broad- 
casting changed hands in a $484 
million management -led LBO. 
Malrite Communications is pres- 
ently in the process of an LBO 
valued in excess of $170 million. 
NAB officials toldR &R this week 
they are concerned about a possi- 
ble nexus between Markey's plan- 
ned probe of LBOs and a move to 
reinstate anti -trafficking rules, but 
subcommittee counsel Larry Irv- 
ing said there is no connection at 
this time. 
"We haven't really thought 
about looking at it from that per- 
spective," he said. "It may well be 
a good opportunity. We've just got 
so much to do with everything else: 
the Fairness Doctrine, children's 
television, cable, must -carry. 
We've got about as full an agenda 
as you could possibly have for the 
next two years ... It's obviously 
something [Markey] cares about, 
it's just that we haven't scheduled 
anything on it at this time." 
House Energy & Commerce 
Committee Chairman John Dingell 
(D -MI), another critic of broadcast 
mergers, has announced plans to 
press ahead for legislation to 
strengthen stockholder rights and 
toughen disclosure rules for take- 
overs. Senate Finance Committee 
Chairman Lloyd Bentsen (D-TX) 
also plans extensive hearings on 
the use of junk bonds to take com- 
panies private. 
Acquisitions Fuel 
Radio Growth 
According to a new study by the 
investment banking firm of Ver- 
onis, Suhler & Associates, the top 
five radio groups in terms of 
revenue growth in 1987 were Sage 
Broadcasting (up 144.3% to $8.8 
million), Jacor Communications 
(up 86.6% to $44 million), Emmis 
Broadcasting (up 75.1% to $58.9 
million), Infinity Broadcasting (up 
60.7% to $74.1 million), and West- 
wood One (up 47.1% to $87.2 mil- 
lion). Those dramatic increases 
were largely the result of major ac- 
quisition programs undertaken by 
the groups, some of which used so- 
called junk bonds to fuel their ex- 
pansion. 
The five largest radio broad- 
casting groups in terms of revenue, 
according to Veronis Suhler, were: 
Westwood One ($87.2 million), In- 
finity Broadcasting ($74.1 million), 
Metropolitan Broadcasting Co. 
($70.2 million), Emmis Broad- 
casting ($58.9 million), and EZ 
Communications ($47 million). It 
should be noted that Westwood's 
1987 revenue was derived from its 
radio network and syndication op- 
erations; the company did not own 
any radio stations until earlier this 
year when it acquired KIQQ /Los 
Angeles, WYNY -FM /New York, 
and 50% of WNEW /New York.

RAB Projects Radio 
Revenue Increase 
The RAB, in a year -end analysis, is predicting that ra- 
dio advertising revenues will grow 7.8% in 1989 for a total 
of $8.4 billion. 
Local advertising revenues are 
expected to grow 8.5% to $6.5 bil- 
lion. Spot radio is projected to in- 
crease 5.5% for a total of $1.4 bil- 
lion. Network radio revenue is ex- 
pected to grow at a slower 4.5% 
rate for a total of $394 million (see 
chart) . 
RAB is calculating total 1988 rev- 
enues will reach $7.83 billion, for a 
7.4% increase over the previous 
year. The estimates are based on 
ten months of actual figures col- 
lected by the RAB's Local Revenue 
Pool, Radio Expenditure Reports, 
and the Radio Network Associa- 
tion. 
"Radio has enjoyed a year of 
steady growth," said RAB Presi- 
dent William Stakelin. "Local 
advertising, which accounts for 77 
cents of every dollar we earn, set 
the pace this year with increases of 
7.9% over 1987. Network radio is 
rebounding from a slump in the 
early part of 1988 and should close 
out 1.7% ahead of last year. Na- 
tional spot radio grew faster than 
we originally estimated, to close 
the year 6.8% beyond the 1987 
totals. Spot's progress should con- 
tinue into 1989." 
The RAB study assumes a 2.5% 
growth in gross national product 
during 1989, a figure reflecting un- 
certainty about future economic 
conditions. The trade group says 
radio broadcasters can expect to 
operate in an economy charact- 
erized by slower growth in con- 
sumer spending and fixed business 
investment. The group expects an 
inflation rate of five percent during 
1989, with escalating wage de- 
mands in an economy with 5.5% 
unemployment putting upward 
pressure on prices. The group also 
expects interest rates will climb 
during the early part of 1989, with a 
peak by mid -year. 
"The jury is still out on the ques- 
tion of a recession, but prudent 
businesspeople know that `what 
goes up must come down' - some- 
time," Stakelin said. 
NEWS BRIEFS 
GAF Can Keep WNCN, 
Must Pay $2.6 Million 
The New York Court of Appeals has 
affirmed a lower court ruling that will al- 
low GAF Corp. to retain ownership of 
Classical powerhouse WNCN/New 
York but requires the company to pay 
$2.6 million to a company that held an 
option on the station. 
The ruling is the latest development 
in a dispute that dates to 1976, when 
then -GAF managers gave Concert Ra- 
dio, Inc., an option to buy WNCN for 
$2.9 million if GAF decided to sell the 
station within five years. In return, Con- 
cert, which was backed by two lis- 
teners groups that sought the return of 
a Classical format to WNCN, dropped 
its competing application for the sta- 
tion. In late 1980 GAF announced 
plans to sell WNCN. While GAF even- 
tually dropped that plan, Concert 
argued that its option had been ac- 
tivated by the company's initial sale an- 
nouncement. 
been triggered by GAF's announce- 
ment, GAF has more than met its 
primary contractual obligation by retain- 
ing WNCN's Classical format for the 
past 12 years. 
NTIA To Move? 
The National Telecommunications 
and Information Administration 
(NTIA), which is responsible for advis- 
ing the administration on international 
and domestic telecommunications pol- 
icy, may become part of the newly -cre- 
ated Technology Administration under 
a soon -to -begin reorganization of the 
Commerce Department. NTIA chief Al- 
bert Sikes currently reports directly to 
the Secretary of Commerce. 
Critics say the loss of access to the 
Cabinet level of government would di- 
minish NTIA's effectiveness as an inde- 
pendent policy voice. 
A final decision on NTIA's fate is ex- 
pected sometime in the next few 
weeks.

monstrous "Bosszilla" 
once replaced by the democratic, 
caring, benign, patient, boss -as- 
team- player - is back, inspiring 
fear in his employees. Now that the 
change has been made, the ques- 
tion becomes "is fear an effective 
management tool ?" 
According to New York -based 
BFS Psychological Assoc. Chair- 
man Mortimer Feinberg, the an- 
swer is "yes" - if it is the right 
kind of fear. In fact, since authority 
means power, and power inspires 
fear, the boss who doesn't assert 
his authority loses it. 
Focused Vs. 
Free- Floating Fear 
Feinberg claims that there are 
two kinds of managerial fear: 
"free- floating" and "focused." Of 
the two, "focused fear" can be an 
effective management tool be- 
cause it not only instills fear, but 
What Price 
Business 
Travel?

of attending out -of -town 
conventions, conclaves, 
seminars, and other such 
events was $672. The follow- 
ing chart breaks out the amount 
of money spent by US corn - 
panies on business trips as well 
as the percentage of firms

supplies the individual with con- 
structive ways to get rid of that 
fear - it creates a "defiant" fear 
that motivates people to positive 
action. 
The "free- floating" fear, on the 
other hand, is a poor tool. Feinberg 
describes this method as "chron- 
ic," casting its victims (your staff) 
into a constant state of anxiety. 
The major drawback to this tech- 
nique is that it keeps your people 
scared, and scared people don't 
think straight - mistakes will be 
made. 
When To Use Focused Fear 
Once you have separated the two 
methods, you'll find that there are 
at least three situations that call 
for a healthy dose of focused fear: 
In an emergency. When dead- 
lines are closing in and your people 
are in a "think tank" or let's -kick- 
the- idea -around mode, a direct 
command to "just DO it ... or 
else" will make them focus on de- 
tail and execution, and they'll get 
the job done. 
In performance reviews. Tell- 
ing an employee that his perform- 
ance is below standard will natur- 
ally scare him. Since the purpose of 
the review is to help the employee 
improve, you should temper the 
fear-creating criticism with an 
agreed -to plan for his improve- 
ment. 
To help cure personal prob- 
lems. Coddling alcoholic and drug 
abusing employees will not help 
cure them or make them produc- 
tive staffers; a shot of fear will. 
The fear of losing their job is often 
the only stimulus that'll reach 
these people. 
Foibles Of Fear Fallout 
The biggest problem with using 
fear as a management technique is 
that it may lead to longterm re- 
sentment toward the fear -inspiring 
boss. There are, however, a couple 
of methods the "Bosszilla" can use 
to minimize this reaction. 
First of all, the fear should be 
made situational, not personal. 
This way, the employee is afraid of 
the consequence of his own actions, 
not of the boss himself. Secondly, 
once the jolt of fear has done its du- 
ty, congratulate the employee on 
getting the job done. 
Use Your Fax 
To Take Orders 
Today there are approxi- 
mately one million fax ma- 
chines in the US workplace, 
a figure that's expected to top three 
million by 1991, so it's time to start 
thinking about new ways to use the 
devices. 
Writing in the NYC -based DM 
News, Stan Fenvessy suggests us- 
ing fax machines to process orders. 
After all, fax machines can not on- 
ly take orders 24 hours a day, but 
also are less-expensive than either 
overnight delivery services or toll - 
free telephone orders.

SALES STRATEGY 
Interviewing & Testing New Salespeople 
One of the most critical, not to mention toughest, 
jobs a manager has to face is hiring the right per- 
son for a sales position. Errors in this department 
are both costly and easy to make. This week, we'll cover 
two specific areas - interviewing and testing - that 
might help you to hire the right person. Next week, we'll 
take a look at the best places to find potential applicants as 
well as other tips that will help you avoid common hiring 
mistakes. 
Specific Interview 
Techniques 
Before beginning the interview 
process, both you and the applicant 
should have a realistic outline of 
what the job will entail on a daily 
basis. You should avoid such sim- 
plistic textbook lines as "Your job 
is to cultivate and develop revenue 
from both new and existing adver- 
tisers." If you're hiring this person 
to really beat the bushes looking 
for new accounts, then isolate and 
explain that fact. 
The next step is to present the 
applicant with actual case studies 
of new salespeople who've started 
at your station under similar condi- 
tions. All you have to do is graph 
your salespeople's revenue- gener- 
ating success during their first 
year of employment. Out of four or 
five case studies, you'll likely find 
one who's done exceptionally well, 
a couple who did moderately well, 
and a couple who are - as we say 
- "no longer with the station, and 
pursuing other sales opportunities." 
Breaking It Down 
Next, you'll want to break down 
the job components actually need- 
ed to come up with the required 
revenue. In their simplest, most 
realistic form these components 
are: generating leads, setting up 
appointments, making face -to-face 
sales calls, and closing the deals. 
Keep in mind that it's absolutely 
essential to think through the actu- 
al execution of each of these steps, 
including the amount of time that 
needs to be devoted to each one. 
Determine whether any of these 
steps will include such necessities 
as cold calls, library research, or 
joining groups and associations. 
You'll also want to explain what 
will actually be required to gener- 
ate a sufficient number of appoint- 
ments. For example, you may 
want new people to primarily spend 
their first week on the phone, ob- 
taining new business appoint- 
ments. (Being new to the telephone 
game, they'll probably close only 
one in ten people upon seeing them 
in person.) Explain that in the 
following weeks they'll wind up 
spending at least three hours a day 
on the phone, and be expected to 
see at least five people a day. 
Qualifying Senior 
Salespeople 
When jobs arise that need to be 
filled by an experienced radio 
salesperson, there are several ad- 
ditional items you'll find impor- 
tant. First, isolate the job responsi- 
bilities and work habits that are 
critical to you. For example, if ev- 
eryone at your station is responsi- 
ble for cultivating new business, 
then what percentage of new bill- 
ing will this individual be responsi- 
ble for each month? Second, it's 
important to clearly define what 
you mean by new business. If you 
don't, you may discover that the 
new salesperson has a different 
definition; i.e., new activity from 
an account that hasn't historically 
bought radio advertising. Is this 
"new business" to you? 
You'll also find it's important to 
actually delineate the percentage 
of increase that you expect from 
"Hiring the right person is probably the most 
important part of a sales manager's job, and it 
will ultimately make the difference in your 
overall success or failure." 
Don't hesistate to show potential 
employees the actual realities of 
the job - and don't be afraid to 
scare people away. The last thing 
you want is to hire someone you 
feel is qualified, only to have that 
person grow disillusioned within 
the first couple of weeks. Hiring the

manager's job, and it will ultimate- 
ly make the difference in your 
overall success or failure. 
It's better to paint the worst 
scenario imaginable - even if the 
recruit later finds the job not as 
bad as it was made out to be - 
rather than having the new em- 
ployee become disillusioned, un- 
motivated, and, ultimately, in your 
office every day asking for new 
leads.

taining current business. When 
presenting this, you should specif- 
ically state what might happen 
(e.g., he'll lose the account) if this 
percentage increase isn't achieved. 
Ibo often, managers don't specif- 
ically communicate the increases 
they expect from traditional sta- 
tion advertisers. Thus, when it's 
time for annual negotiations, sales- 
people often settle for the account's 
traditional negotiating technique: 
"Our radio budget has been cut 
back. No one is getting any in- 
creases. And we need additional 
considerations from everyone." 
However, in every one of these 
cases you'll still find stations that 
walk away from the negotiating ta- 
By Chris Beck 
ble with additional budget in- 
creases year after year. Ensure 
that your station is among them by 
specifying that's what you expect. 
Testing Work Habits 
No matter what the job entails, 
it's possible to test an applicant's 
skills. Radio PDs rely on airchecks 
and actual listening. Secretaries 
are put through typing drills and 
other special skills tests. Salespeo- 
ple, on the other hand, are usually 
interviewed and that's it. 
You can dramatically increase 
your hiring success ratio by testing 
sales applicants' actual skills and 
work habits. While it's generally 
impossible for you to actually go on 
calls with each of them, there are 
some effective ways to get a handle 
on a prospective salesperson's 
work habits and knowledge of the 
skills that are important to success 
on the job. Some examples: 
Test how well they think on 
their feet by having job finalists in- 
terviewed by all or several of your 
current salespeople. 
Test work habits by asking 
them to examine the appointments 
they've made at their current job 
during the last month, and have 
them make a list of every face-to- 
face appointment they've had dur- 
izg that time. After they've corn - 
pleted the list, ask them to isolate 
the purpose of each appointment. 
Were they "first -time new business 
appointments," "new advertiser 
closing calls," or "existing adver- 
tiser /agency service calls ?" 
Ask to see copies of their pro- 
posals for new business as well as 
renewals. 
Have them bring a list of their 
current or previous accounts. In- 
dependently make calls to several 
people on the list, either asking 
generic questions about salespeo- 
ple in general, or more specific 
inquiries about the salesperson in 
question. This relatively small in- 
vestment of time can give you a 
tremendous amount of critical in- 
formation that couldn't be obtained 
by simply relying on references 
supplied by the applicant. 
Kustomized 
Kalling Kards 
C 
ustomized cards - which 
can be used for a variety of 
notes to clients - are a sim- 
ple, but effective selling resource to 
have available to your sales staff. 
KROQILos Angeles supplies the 
sort of glossy, high -quality, four - 
color cards pictured to its salespeo- 
ple for use in all those situations 
where a simple note can make a big 
impression. 
Testing Sales Skills 
You can also test actual sales 
skills in one of the following ways: 
Have applicants answer tradi- 
tional objections they might hear 
from prospective accounts. Have 
at least ten common objections and 
excuses on hand, such as "I'm not 
interested" ... "I only buy news- 
paper ads" ... "Call me back in 30 
days" ... "Let me think about it" 
... This is too expensive" . . 
"Your cost per point is too high," 
etc. 
Give the applicant a list of 
three people to call in your pres- 
ence, and ask him to see if he can 
make an appointment with each 
one. 
Using a proposal that the job 
seeker has brought along to the in- 
terview, role -play an actual closing 
sequence with the applicant. 
The better organized you are in 
testing actual sales skills during an 
interview, the better you communi- 
cate what is actually expected - 
and the greater your hiring success 
ratio will be in the long run.

31/2 -Inch Versions 
To Dominate Market 
Bigger isn't necessarily bet- 
ter, especially when it 
comes to computer disc 
drives. Although 51/4-inch models 
are currently the standard for 
hard -disc drives, a recent report 
fromDisc /Trend Inc. predicts that 
the 31/2-inch hard -disc drive will 
boss the market by the end of next 
year. 
One of the major reasons for this 
change is that improved technolo- 
gy has raised the capacity of these 
small drives to almost 300 mega- 
bytes, or 300 million characters of 
data. Disc /Trend also predicts that 
84.5% of the disc drives in the 100-to 
300- megabyte categories will be 
3 1/2-inches by 1991 - an amazing 
jump, considering this percentage 
stood at a mere 2.8% in 1987. 
The company also notes that 51/4- 
inch drives won't vanish, but will 
find other markets, such as the $4 
million mainframe disc market in 
which IBM has been using 14 -inch 
drives since the early 1960s. Fur- 
thermore, Disc /Trend predicts 
that IBM will add 51/4-inch drives to 
its "System /370" mainframes next 
year in an effort to save substantial 
space in crowded computer rooms.

Motion(less) Pictures On TV 
With the exception of Polaroid prints, photographers have never 
been able to view their pictures immediately after shooting them. 
For years, camera buffs have desired a camera that can record 
photos on a magnetic disc and then play them back on a TV set or monitor. 
Such cameras have existed in the past, but - at a cost of $2000 or more 
- they've generally been out of the price range of the ordinary amateur 
photographer. 
All that is about to change, however, when Canon Inc. introduces its 
new "filmless" camera (the "RC- 250 ") this coming January. The camera - 
which resembles a sleek pair of binoculars - records images on a two -inch 
magnetic disc that can store up to 50 photos. 
After each or all pictures, the camera can then be hooked up to your 
TV for a viewing of the photos. Push a "fast forward" button on the camera, 
and the pictures speed away as though you were watching a carousel of 
slides. (You can also send the disc to Canon to have prints made.) 
One major advantage to Canon's new system is that it doesn't require a 
separate playback unit - your existing TV set will do just fine. Suggested 
retail price for the camera will be about $800: the discs will be sold in- 
dividually for $10 each.

Australia's 1988 Hit List 
We've been running World Music Overview charts 
since mid- January, and that presents a unique opportuni- 
s 
CMJ, Dance Music Report, and 
the Record , the publications that 
supply the new rock tracks, dance 
tracks, and Canadian charts for 
World Music Overview, will, I'm 
sure, compile their own year -end 
charts from the unabridged ver- 
sions of their charts. Similarly, 
MRIB, which supplies our UK 
chart, can do the same thing easily 
I wouldn't presume to preempt 
them by throwing together year- 
end tallies from the information 
they lend us for WMO. 
But our Australian chart is an- 
other story. As I've mentioned be- 
fore, it's compiled from Top 10 air- 
play and new add lists of Australi- 
an artists only supplied by eight of 
the country's top -rated FM AOR/ 
CHR hybrid stations. This would 
appear to be the perfect time to 
acknowledge the help of those sta- 
tions and thank them for faithfully 
contributing their lists every week 
(by fax) to bring you the most up- 
to -date look at what's going on in 
Australian music available any- 
where. Congratulations on pro- 
viding almost a year's worth of info 
to: 
SA -FM /Adelaide 
FM104 /Brisbane 
KIX106 /Canberra 
EON -FM /Melbourne 
FOX -FM /Melbourne 
96F M/Perth 
2- DAY /Sydney 
2MMM /Sydney 
What I'm getting at is that with 
almost a year's worth of charts in 
the bag (January 22 to November 
25 plus an unpublished January 15 
test run), we can come up with a 
year -end chart of Australia's top 
hits as programmed by the na- 
tion's leading rock stations. (Next 
year we'll use data from 12/2/88 
through 11/24/89, as with the rest of 
R&R 's year -end charts.) 
And that's what you see at top 
right, the Top 40 Australian rock 
hits. American labels have been 
added if the song has been released 
here by the end of November, and 
it's easy to see at a glance which 
labels are investing in Australian 
artists. If any labels here have 
plans to release some of the other 
artists listed in '89, let me know, 
and I'll pass the info along.

INXS: Australia's top artists 
Crowded House nipped the 
Church in a tight race (the chart 
was calculated, by the way, on 
position points accumulated on the 
WMO Australian Top 10 chart 
throughout the year). Nos. 3 and 4 
have not been released here yet, 
although RCA is set to issue John 
Farnham in early '89. 1927 is a new 
group in a pop -styled vein. The rest 
of the Top 10 has been out here, so 
I'll cruise through the rest of the 
Top 40, supplying comments when 
I know something about the artist 
(not a guarantee) . 
Daryl Braithwaite at #12 is the 
former lead singer of '70s Aussie 
stars Sherbet (also known here as 
Highway and the Sherbs) ; he also 
had a successful concurrent solo 
career when Sherbet was riding 
high. The Choirboys are hard 
rockers, while Rockmelons boast 
more of a dance groove. Speaking 
of "groove," the Eurogliders are 
continuing to explore the dance/ 
funk realms they introduced on 
their last domestic Columbia 
release a couple years ago. 
Chantoozies are a female pop act 
described reasonably accurately 
as Australia's Bananarama. Some 
Crowded House: #1 in Australia 
of our reporters play them and 
Kylie Minogue, others find them 
too far over the pop line. The An- 
gels are the same hard -rocking 
group that had several LPs out 
here as Angel City, and in fact 
recently released a sampler from 
the live LP from which their #29 hit 
here was taken on a small US label 
called Telegraph. "Face Again" is 
not on the sampler, however. 
The Hippos sounded to me like 
some form of intellectual rockabil- 
Church: longevity champs 
ly on "Dark Age," while the Black 
Sorrows started as a zydeco-flavor- 
ed spinoff from former AOR cult 
favesJo Jo Zep & The Falcons and 
have since moved into a straighter 
pop -rock sound. The Go-Betweens, 
whose LP containing "Streets Of 
Your Town" just came out onCapi- 
tol, have been a cult favorite in 
England for years but have not 
done much in Australia until now.

many hit tracks over the year that 
they finished 1 -2 going away on the 
Artists list - no one else was close.

Thirteen of the Top 20 artists had 
their current records released in 
the States in '88, a pretty impres- 
sive showing for Australian artists' 
global impact. INXS, Icehouse, the 
Church, and Kylie Minogue (not to 
mention Midnight Oil) all had solid 
CHR hits, while Little River Band

COPELAND, KEITH EMERSON, ex -CLASH man PAUL 
SIMENON, and even members of SIGUE SIGUE SPUT- 
NIK joining in on the axe session, which must have been 
quite a sight!

London is bracing itself for the 
arrival of JERRY LEE LEWIS on 
January 9. He'll be here in his role 
as "creative consultant" for the bi- 
ograpltcal film, "Great Balls Of 
Fire," starring RANDY QUAID. 
With the Memphis scenes already 
in the can, filming moves to Lon- 
don to center on the big controver- 
sy of 1958 when Lewis arrived here 
with his 13- year -old cousin bride 
and almost destroyed his career. 
On a sad note, Annie Lennox 
is recovering from the loss of her 
baby who was stillborn in London 
last weekend. We wish her well. 
PREFAB SPROUT fans will be 
pleased to hear that "Protest 
Songs," the group's lost LP of 1985, 
will finally be released following an 
American remix by MICHAEL 
BRAUER. Leader PADDY 
McALOON hopes the LP will be in 
the shops by April. Meanwhile, the 
Sprouts have a number of other 
projects on tap, including an LP of 
Christmas songs with guest vocal- 
ists for next year and a soundtrack 
for a musical. 
BILLY BRAGG ended his two 
concerts at London's Dominion 
Theatre last week with encores of 
the SMITHS' "Panic" and a 
PRINCE parody, "Acid Rain."

NAUGHTY STUDIO SEXCAPADES 
Crazed Cuckold Crunches Car 
Even knowing how fanatic golfers can be about their 
game, I was impressed with one player who woke up long 
before sunrise and carried his clubs to a radio station hi 
the Deep South. In silence, he waited inside his car until the 
morning personality drove into the parking lot. Then, as 
the story goes, he jumped out, chose just the right club, 
and shattered the morning man's windshield. Kids, can 
you say cuckold? 
Cuckold, as a noun, is defined as 
"a man whose wife has committed 
adultery." In our little anecdote, 
it's defined as a golfer who was un- 
der the impression that his wife 
was doing more than just talking to 
a talk show host, himself a married 
man who shall, of course, remain 
anonymous, because we radio peo- 
ple are a tight -knit, self- protective 
little clan of professionals bent on 
avoiding lawsuits and physical 
beatings. 
(By the way, did you know that 
in some cultures in the Far East 
there is actually a hand signal that 
signifies cuckoldry? The late Walt 
Disney found that out the hard way 
when he exported a Mickey Mouse 
cartoon to the Orient. The cartoon 
had a scene in which the rodent 
stuck his thumbs in his ears and 
fluttered his fingers around. Over 
here, that's just an innocent 
gesture that means something like, 
"Yah yah yah on you." Over 
there, it means "Your wife is 
screwing around." The cartoon 
was quickly pulled for editing.) 
But let's get back to the general 
theme of studio-spawned sex and 
how it can get you clubbed, killed, 
or even worse. 
At this point, I would like to tell 
you about a number of enlightening 
personal experiences in which a 
variety of love -starved listeners, 
ranging up to (and even exceed- 
ing! ) 400 pounds, have connived to 
get me into various homes, pools, 
cars, bars and a Spandex tightrope 
costume. Yes, I would like to tell 
you, but, uh, there's insufficient 
column space for that. Yeah, that's 
it. (We'll talk at the next conven- 
tion, perhaps while wearing rec- 
tangular black masks covering our 
eyes.) 
In closing, I suppose that any 
mention of a fellow broadcaster's 
suspected improprieties - such as 
our talk show guy who came close 
to being hooked and sliced by the 
golf nut - should rightfully include 
a disclaimer that not only endorses 
high moral standards, but goes on 
to mention the various personal 
and legal liabilities inherent in il- 
licit sex. 
Instead, perhaps I'll just recom- 
mend a couple of videos: "Play 
Misty for Me" and "Fatal Attrac- 
tion." 
Washington At Valley Forge 
MONDAY, DECEMBER 19 - George Washington and his revolutionary army began the famous winter 
encampment at Valley Forge, Pennsylvania in 1777. Today the historic march will be reenacted, with "living history 
demonstrations" at the National Historical Park at Valley Forge. Call (215) 783 -7700. 
Putting a real chill on Christmas shopping, the prime interest rate was raised to a record 21.5 percent in 1980. 
Corrugated paper was patented in 1871. During the War of 1812, the British captured Ft. Niagara in 1813. 
Birthdays: Jennifer Beals 25. Tim Reid 44. Ceclly Tyson 49. Baseball Hall of Famer Al Kaline 54. 
Zodiac Killer At Large 
TUESDAY, DECEMBER 20 - The first victims of the San Francisco -area Zodiac Killer, a man and woman shot to 
death inside a parked car, were discovered 20 years ago (1968). Police would like to question him about 40 other 
murders in Western states. 
A New York court ruled in 1984 that it is illegal for a husband to rape his wife. Russia's 14 countries consolidated as the 
Union of Soviet Socialist Republics in 1922. South Carolina became the first state to secede from the Union in 1860. 
Birthdays: Peter Criss 41. John Hillerman 56 (Jonathan Higgins in "Magnum, P.I. "). 
First Day Of Winter 
WEDNESDAY, DECEMBER 21 - Winter begins at 10:28 EST this morning. The year's longest night is tonight, 
and the shortest day of 1988 is tomorrow. 
Ten years ago, the first of 33 bodies was found under mass murdererJohn Gacy's house in Chicago (1968). Forty 
years ago, Ireland declared itself a republic, rather than British dominion, and withdrew from the Commonwealth (1948). 
75th anniversary of the first crossword puzzle, published in the New York World newspaper in 1913. It is Forefathers 
Day in New England, commemorating the Pilgrims coming ashore from the "Mayflower" in 1620 at Plymouth, 
Massachusetts. 
Birthdays: Chris Evert Lloyd 34. Carl Wilson 42. Frank Zappa 48. Jane Fonda 51. Phil Donahue 53. 
First Electric Tree 
THURSDAY, DECEMBER 22 - Ed Johnson switched on the world's first Christmas tree with electric lights at his 
home in New York City in 1882. He was an associate of light bulb inventor Thomas Edison. 
Bernhard Goetz shot and wounded four teenagers on a New York City subway in 1984. The Beatles' Christmas show in 
Liverpool sold out 25 years ago (1963). International Arbor Day, encouraging the planting of trees. Annual Ursid meteor 
shower tonight. 
Birthdays: Maurice & Robin Gibb 39. Steve Garvey 40. Diane Sawyer 43. Lady Bird Johnson 76. 
Around The World In Nine Days 
FRIDAY, DECEMBER 23 - "Voyager" flew into the aviation record books in 1986 when it completed its nonstop, 
nine -day flight around the world on a single load of fuel. Five hours before landing one engine died, but the other one 
kept working. 
A 6.2 earthquake claimed 5000 victims in Nicaragua in 1972. Clement Moore's poem "Visit From St. Nicholas (The 
Night Before Christmas)" was published in 1823. Full Cold Moon.

Reading The Mail 
Grappling With Racism, The Decline Of Personality, 
And Community Involvement 
The letters I receive often raise interesting and impor- 
tant issues. This week I'd like to share several that con- 
cern major problems specific to UC. 
Ignoring The Black Market 
Joyner Communications, Inc. 
President Tom Joyner copied me 
on the following letter to MCI Tele- 
communications Regional Manag- 
er Tom Davis: 
My rep firm in New York ad- 
vises me that MCI Telecommuni- 
cations, through its agency Wells, 
Rich, Greene, is placing its adver- 
tising with the proviso that no 
Black or UC stations are to be pur- 
chased. I believe this to be a seri- 
ous mistake, both in substance and 
form. 
There is a vast upscale black 
market in America that is being 
totally ignored by the MCI plan. 
This audience is valuable and 
large. My company has significant 
research and will be happy to 
make it available to MCI. 
Frankly, we are finding outdated 
ideas among some accounts and ad 
agencies that still consider the 
black market to be composed en- 
tirely of slaves and lackeys. 
Nothing could be further from the 
truth. This is one company which 
considers no black' instructions to 
be highly racist. 
I look forward to your response. 
'Dime A Dozen Syndrome' 
Paul "Hit Man" Hickey, an air 
personality at WKXI /Jackson, MS, 
addressed the decline of personali- 
ty in UC and Black radio: 
Many thanks for your insights on 
personality in Black/Urban radio. 
As a professional radio announcer/ 
personality, I think a few things 
need to be said regarding your arti- 
cle of 10/21. 
Black /Urban radio has indeed 
suffered a personality decline these 
last few years in what was once an 
"everybody is a star" industry. Yet 
with the advent of the so-called spe- 
cialized formats and concern about 
what's right for the market, radio 
jocks have fallen into the "jocks 
are a dime a dozen" syndrome. 
Where does the problem start? Is 
there anything anyone can do to 
correct it? Maybe we can start at 
the broadcast schools or at colleges 
that turn out mass communica- 
tions majors. 
Having worked in major mar- 
kets and now in a small market, I 
know everyone dreams of the big 
time. Yet the big time isn't all it's 
cut out to be. I've learned from my 
peers that no matter where you are 
or what you are doing, you're still a 
personality. 
'A Dying Art Form' 
Bobby Jay, currently an air per- 
sonality at WCBS -FM /New York, 
decried the the past and present 
state of Black radio. Here are ex- 
cerpts from his letter:

LISTENERS JUST WANT TO HAVE FUN 
Creative Contests 
One of the funniest bits I've heard in a while was done 
by WALY /Altoona, PA 's Steve Willett . It was a contest 
sort of - that satirized a well-known TV game show. 
I asked Willett to explain the 
genesis of this and other creative 
WALY contests: 
"WALY 104 signed on in March 
1987, with no money and no clients. 
Without ratings, management had 
to attract clients as best they could 
- usually with good of `trade.' Our 
trade became our first prize: a free 
breakfast at a cozy little diner. 
"This led to `Sing For Your 
Breakfast!' Contestants would 
choose from among three doors. 
Behind each door was a song they 
would have to sing. The selections 
ranged from operatic versions of 
old standards to contemporary 
hits. 
"A couple of months later, we 
signed a deal with a local theater to 
provide us with an indefinite supp- 
ly of movie passes. This was the be- 
ginning of our `fun contests,' start- 
ing with the `Current Events Quiz.' 
This consisted of a multiple choice 
quiz based on local and national 
news stories, with the listener 
clearly instructed to `Pick [an- 
swer] C.' 
"After three months, I placed the 
`Current Events Quiz' on summer 
hiatus and started a new set of con- 
tests based on real TV game 
shows. `Radio Password' is just 
like the TV show, except that both 
the listener and the contestant hear 
everything - including the secret 
password." 
Radio 
Password 
Here's how WALYIAltoona's 
Steve Willett plays "Radio Pass- 
word": 
WILLETT: You're our contestant 
for "Radio Password!" You know 
the rules; just like TV, you have to 
guess the secret password based 
on our one -word clue. Are you 
ready? 
CALLER: Ready' 
WILLETT: Okay, here's today's 
password. 
ANNOUNCER (sotto voice): The 
password is "typewriter." 
WILLETT: Okay, Sandra. here's 
your clue: "Kumquat." 
CALLER: Umm Typewriter. 
WILLETT: (excited) Typewriter! 
That's correct! 
(Sound effects: crowd cheering). 
Steve Willett 
READING THE MAIL 
Listeners Get 
The Punchlines 
Willett continued, "`Radio Jeop- 
ardy' is also like the TV show - ex- 
cept I tell the listener in advance 
(off the air) what the question will 
be in response to my `answer.' The 
best part of this is listeners deliver 
the punchlines (very well, I might 
add) . It's nice to know your lis- 
teners are in on the gag. 
" `Radio Name That Tune' isn't 
very difficult to play, inasmuch as 
the snippet the contestant hears 
just happens to be the title of the 
song. 
"In these days of `plastic' call-in 
contests, I wanted to stand out with 
contests that are as much fun to 
play as they are to listen to. Plus it 
certainly is a stroke to my ego 
when people stop me on the street 
and say, `Pick C!' "

No Substitute For Dues -Paying 
Reaching into the mailbag this week, I found letters 
from two frustrated novice disc jockeys. The first was in 
response to an aircheck critique that recently appeared in 
this column: 
I'm mad about the aircheck you 
reviewed - "speaking in incom- 
plete sentences, not tying things 
together," etc. Despite all the 
jock's shortcomings, I'm sure 
there will be some station in a big- 
ger market that will come along 
and offer him a job. 
I know I sound better than him. I 
have been in commercial radio for 
five years now, yet I'm still work- 
ing midnights in a tiny market. 
Well, I've had it. When I finish this 
I'm typing up my resignation. I 
can't stand it anymore. Why? 
Because I'm beginning to believe 
what I heard about this business a 
long time ago. It's not what you 
know, but whoyou know. I guess I 
just don't know the right people. 
Shouldering The Blame 
I'm sorry to hear you're giving 
up on radio. But I don't believe you 
can judge whether you "sound bet- 
ter" than another jock based on a 
partial transcript of his show. You 
seem to be blaming anyone and ev- 
eryone but yourself for certain in- 
adequacies in your job package. 
In terms of your resume, you 
don't indicate how long you worked 
at any of the stations mentioned. 
Your college awards (including 
"Most Interesting News Story of 
the Year ") are meaningless to a 
radio professional and only serve 
to emphasize your non -commercial 
background. 
And there's not a PD in the world 
who would consider calling a phar- 
maceutical representative or an 
associate professor of black Ameri- 
can studies for a professional refer- 
ence on a prospective disc jockey. 
Finally, your resume's stated "ob- 
jective" is meaningless: "To gain 
employment that will allow my 
talent to grow and explore." 
Your experience is highly spe- 
cialized (a late -night soft Jazz pro- 
gram) and your style would be ap- 
propriate for relatively few posi- 
tions. You're doing a super laid - 
back voice that many program- 
mers would consider outdated. It's 
unrealistic to expect the PD to 
guess how you would sound in a 
traditional CHR, AC, UC, or Coun- 
try setting. 
You do have an excellent voice, 
but you seem to try too hard to im- 
press your audience with it; you 
pay more attention to voice than to 
content. As a result, there's very 
little one -on-one communication. 
Ready For The Big Time? 
The second letter came from a 
college graduate who had just corn- 
pleted an internship at a well- 
known major market station. He 
also complained about having to 
"know somebody" in a position of 
influence. He concluded by asking, 
"What do you do after that intern- 
ship - without going to Fargo, 
North Dakota ?" 
The radio world is flooded with 
people who have college radio 
broadcasting experience and/or 
degrees, and think they're qual- 
ified for the big time. The world is 
also filled with people who interned 
at large market stations and 
believe smaller stations should 
jump at the chance to hire them. 
But in reality, college radio ex- 
perience is worth next to nothing 
(and a degree in broadcasting or 
communications is worth even 
less) in the eyes of commercial ra- 
dio. And as you undoubtedly learn- 
ed while at Station X, an intern oc- 
cupies the lowest rung on the sta- 
tion ladder. I'm sure it was in- 
teresting and perhaps you learned 
a lot, but it certainly doesn't equip 
you to compete with people who 
have fulltime, commercial radio 
experience. 
Including a business card with 
your resume that describes you as 
a "programming consultant" in- 
vites ridicule by a prospective 
employer. Many people would look 
at your resume and think, "What 
qualifies this guy to be a program- 
ming consultant ?" 
Real World 
Experience A Must 
If you're looking for work as a 
disc jockey, you might very well 
have to start in a market consider- 
ably smaller than Fargo. There 
simply is no substitute for real on- 
air experience. If you seriously 
wish to pursue a radio career, my 
advice is: stop looking for short- 
cuts, get a fulltime DJ gig in a 
small market, and start paying 
your dues.

comments, and cassette airchecks 
are welcome. Due to the large 
volume of mail, however, I regret

receive.

Cash, Shelton, Mattea 
& Raven Receive Honors 
Country stars Rosanne Cash, Ricky Van Shelton, 
Kathy Mattea, and Eddy Raven are all recent awards 
recipients. 
Cash's "Tennessee Flat Top 
Box" was chosen by the Amuse- 
ment & Music Operators Associa- 
tion as the "Jukebox Country 
Record Of the Year." AMOA mem- 
bers selected winners reflecting 
the top revenue producers between 
August '87 and '88. 
Columbia labelmate Shelton tied 
with pop singer Rick Astley for the 
"Rising Star" award, picked by the 
AMOA's Board of Directors. 
Mattea has been nominated for 
the "Outstanding Young Woman of 
America" award by the 23- year -old 
organization of the same name. 
The awards recognize women 
whose "time, talents, and dedica- 
tion have enriched the quality of 
American life." 
Raven was surprised onstage 
when he received the "Governor's 
Award" from his native state of 
Louisiana during a concert at Red 
River Revel in Shreveport. The 
presentation on behalf of Governor 
Buddy Roemer cited Raven's 
"outstanding performance world- 
wide in the field of music and 
entertainment." 
Celeb Book Published 
Alan= Nash has published "Be- 
hind Closed Doors" (Knopf/ New 
York), a book of interviews with 
Country music personalities. Each 
of the 27 artists is introduced by a 
brief bio, followed by excerpts of 
conversations with the author. Art- 
ists included are Emmylou Harris, 
Dolly Parton, Merle Haggard, Re- 
ba McEntire, Willie Nelson, Ala- 
bama, and Rosanne Cash. The 
author has also written "Dolly," a 
biography of Parton, and "Golden 
Girl: The Story Of Jessica Sav- 
itch," as well as numerous maga- 
zine articles. 
TheCountry Music Foundation 
has published "Country: The Mu- 
sic And The Musicians" (Abbey - 
ville Press), a 592 -page book of es- 
says edited by Paul Kingsbury. In- 
cluded are 800 photos, 16 chapters, 
and a slew of contributing authors 
writing on topics from historical 
figures to trends in the country mu- 
sic industry.

To all those special people who helped

and dedication and send my best wishes for this Holiday Season and

20VC: Mac the VC on the Journey from Homeless To Becoming A VC, What It Takes To Raise a Fund on Twitter, Why the Venture World is F***** Up and How Institutional LPs Need To Change
20VC
Nov 01, 2021
Share
McKeever "Mac" Conwell II is the founder and managing partner of RareBreed Ventures, a pre-seed fund that invests outside of large tech ecosystems, with a concentrated portfolio approach being the first check with up to $250K. Mac's journey into venture is nothing short of inspirational, Mac went from being homeless to being an engineer to founding his own companies to today, raising Rarebreed largely on Twitter.
In Today’s Episode with Mac the VC You Will Learn:
1.) How Mac went from being homeless to becoming an engineer and starting his own company? How did his time operating lead to his becoming a VC and building his Twitter brand?
2.) What are the biggest ways that venture is messed up today? Why does Mac believe it does not matter about getting into hot deals? Why does Mac believe that the brand of the VC that does your round does not matter? Does Mac see the leading venture brands investing outside SF and NYC? What elements of an investment compel them more than others?
3.) In the wake of the George Floyd event, who does Mac note did not say anything? How does Mac want to see diversity introduced at the institutional LP level? What does Mac believe institutional LPs care about? What can institutional LPs do structurally to allow themselves to invest in the next generation of emerging managers?
4.) Why does Mac not like AngelList Rolling Funds? How did he structure his fund in a creative way? How does Mac feel about the requirements for GP commits? How did Mac use Twitter very specifically to raise his fund? Which people went out of their way to help him? What were some of the biggest takeaways from those discussions?
