a consumer renaissance. I like that. Let's go. Nice. KJ, thank you for coming on the pod today. I want to jump right in. Decided to talk about everything consumer and AI. You're one of the top experts in the space, experience at Forerunner and also at Google Ventures. And now you're a partner there. And each week you actually write a column about consumer. So you are the perfect person to ask, what is the current state of consumer and what is everyone missing?

[SPEAKER_00]
Well, first, you're entirely too kind. And I appreciate you inviting me onto the podcast. And it's funny that you highlight the column. It's actually a really fun collaboration that we have with one of our advisors. His name is David Benjamin, who might be the only person I know who probably spends more time in the darkest corners of the internet than I do. And so ends up being some really fun conversations. And so, yeah, those columns are weekly musings, so to speak. But yeah, to answer your question, consumer AI. I think the funny thing about consumer, especially when you ask a lot of other investors, is that it's been a bit of a bad word recently. A lot of people have been spooked. A lot of people have missed a lot of bets. Even some of the bets that they've taken haven't necessarily panned out. And I would argue that the reason for that has a lot to do with just human nature. I think human beings are largely fixed. Like, I don't think we've evolved much in the last two years. I don't think we've evolved much in the last 50. I think what ends up happening is that the tools that we have available to us do change. And I think for a very long time, the tools that we had were kind of good enough. Like, if I needed to go from point A to point B, Uber was more than good. If I needed groceries delivered, DoorDash, Instacart was much more than satisfactory. I think what we're seeing now is something that extends beyond just incremental. And I think AI is kind of the catalyst for that, where you start to see 100,000x improvements over existing consumer experiences. And so I would argue that we're on the cusp of a consumer renaissance. And I'm particularly excited about the new crop of companies that are being forged today. That will be extremely meaningful in the years to come.

[SPEAKER_01]
Wow. I want to just double click on the consumer renaissance. What does that fully look like? Is there like an example? Consumer renaissance is a strong, that's a strong word. And today, there's like a lot of mantras. Totally. From all the columns that you've been doing that I want to jump into. But this mantra, I haven't heard about it. So tell me more about that.

[SPEAKER_00]
Yeah, I think in a lot of ways, the landscape is being reimagined. And there's an abundance. I'm a former consultant. So I think in frameworks, there's an abundance in frameworks that you can kind of apply to the category. I think one fun one to dig into is democratization, right? So if you think about the different eras of technology, I think technologies existed as a tool that democratized access, for example, to a lot of different things that were either prohibitively expensive, or not within the realm of possibility for most people. Case in point, therapy, right? When you think about the first era of tech solving therapeutic needs, it largely looked like a phone book just put online, right? Where you had marketplaces that sought to broker a connection between a patient and a therapist. Over time, you started to see technologies kind of solve to some extent that therapeutic conditioning, where they were able to either support a therapist in running their business, or, you know, being some type of emotional groundedness in the form of, you know, headspace or something to that effect, to support people through their medical journeys. I think if I think about what AI stands to represent today, you can start to play around with AI therapists, right? Where you can have a therapeutic offering wrapped in an AI like experience. And what that solves for is being able to potentially democratize that access to a broader cohort of people who can't necessarily afford, you know, the $400 a visit that therapy usually involves, or may not have schedules that align. So you can start to think of, all right, I'm going through a crisis of some sort, I need support, it's 3am. How do I kind of solve for that? And technology can show up in very different ways than has been the

[SPEAKER_01]
case previously. Wow. Actually, you're skipping ahead on some of my notes here. I want to talk about AI and health. You actually, in one of your other columns, you wrote about AI should make us more human, not less human. So I want to understand how we can leverage AI to have a deeper human experience. And then even maybe another quote that I read in one of your columns was that, folks, this might be a countercultural moment, where we shift from optimize me, which is like AI is very optimized focus, to liberate me. And this was like referring to some folks who might be starting meds today, which is becoming like very ubiquitous, but they will want to get off of meds or whatever type of health things in the future. And like, there's no real off ramp right now. And so there is like a future that looks like, I want AI to liberate me versus like, optimize me.

[SPEAKER_00]
Totally. I think AI to date has found a lot of success in productivity, which is meaningful, and especially in work context. You have a lot of talk about 10x, 100x engineers, which obviously is impressive and powerful and is changing almost the physics of various businesses. As a consumer investor, and as a, you know, an aspiring anthropologist, I'm interested in kind of the cultural underpinnings of technology and what it can solve for. And I like to think of behaviors, I like to think of patterns, I like to think of being able to solve for the human experience. I think one of the realms or dimensions that I get particularly excited about is indeed healthcare, because I think healthcare to date has been some version of emergency triage. Something goes horrendously wrong, and you point to the healthcare system to try to course correct. Sometimes it's too late. Sometimes it requires a ton of resources. And I think it strips patients and people to some extent of their agency. I like the idea of using technology for folks to reclaim a bit of that agency and self-empower, where you move from something that feels entirely reactive to something that feels way more proactive. And there's like a guiding hand along the way to support you in your healthcare journey. And so when I think about solutions like Council Health, which falls within the GV portfolio, when I think about Aura, which was a company that I was involved in back when I was living a previous life of Forerunner Ventures, I love the idea of being able to put technology into the hands of individuals and giving them the tools to be better equipped to solve for the healthcare journey.

[SPEAKER_01]
Wow. I want to, since you brought up Aura, I do want to go into that place too. AI and hardware, if you will, right now. Yeah. So you worked with Aura when you were at Forerunner. I'm curious, and obviously like Aura, many people, I have my whoop on right now, so apologies. But I know a lot of people who wear Aura, they recently just had some big announcements on revenue marks and just like dominated a market. And I think they just came out with like a new version of the ring. I'm curious if you can share any details around just like that experience working with their team, that product, and then consumer hardware in general.

[SPEAKER_00]
Yeah, totally. So consumer hardware, I think inspires the same level of caution that just consumer in general, where if you talk to investors, everyone proclaims that hardware is hard. And I think that's largely true, right? Like I think the facts do remain that oftentimes margins aren't as attractive as software. Iterative cycles look very different. You have to manage manufacturing complexities. There's a long list of things that make hardware categorically difficult. That said, when it works, it can explode. And I think hardware is probably one of the places that's most likely to inspire joy and delight, especially if done well. So, subscribe, unsubscribe, resubscribe, resubscribe, unsubscribe, all that good stuff. Show everybody how amazing we are. Make sure you tell your friends. If you leave us a five-star review with a comment, we may just read it on the podcast. Get yourself in here. You know, we might start doing a mailbag, but the mailbag will be from comments left with five-star reviews. So, make sure you let everybody know how great we are. If you want to email us, hit us up at buildingoutloudpodcast at gmail.com. Don't worry, Liam reads them all and gets to them, you know, so you got to worry about me and my crazy busy inbox schedule and all the good stuff. Make sure you hit us up on Twitter, MacDVC, Lawyer Liam, and we'll see you next time, folks. Peace out, y'all.

[None]
Peace out, y'all.

sources.text:
[SPEAKER_01]
Welcome to another episode of Venture Unlocked, the podcast that takes you behind the scenes of the business of venture capital. I'm your host, Samir Khadji, and today's episode is a special one as we completely scrapped the normal interview format and had a fun water cooler discussion with two of the brightest and most transparent minds in the industry, Roy Bahad of Bloomberg Beta and Matt Conwell of Rare Breed Ventures. We had a great time talking about all of the challenges and opportunities that exist in venture today. Specifically in this episode, we discuss Rare Breed's unique 506C-driven public fundraise, the concept of seeding emerging managers, why GP commit as a percentage of a fund is outdated as a measure of GP alignment, and what they see as the immediate future of tech and venture. Now, without further ado, let's get into the episode to hear all of this and more. Mac and Roy, so great to have you guys on the show.

[SPEAKER_02]
Great to be here. Yeah, fun. I'm happy this came together. I love it when a Twitter plan comes together.

[SPEAKER_01]
I've been super pumped about this episode, both because I love talking about emerging manager and fund ones, but you guys are two of the most transparent people in the universe, really for the benefit of the ecosystem. And a lot of people know who you guys are, but I want to start with you, Mac. You launched Rare Breed, the fundraise recently. Tell us a little bit about the fund and the ethos.

[SPEAKER_00]
Yeah, so Rare Breed, we're raising a $10 million pre-seed to seed fund. Really, our sweet spot is anything sub $10 million post-money valuations. We are doing it under 506C, so I can publicly disclose and talk about it. So you can ask me anything and I can answer anything. At this point, we've soft-circled about half of the $10 million already. We're now starting to send out subscription docs and get people to put money into the fund. Talking about the ethos, I'm really looking to invest in companies primarily outside the major tech hubs, so outside of Silicon Valley, New York, and Massachusetts. We will invest in those areas opportunistically, but that's not where the bulk of the deal flow will come from. And looking to be the first or one of the first investors into every company we invest in, target check size $250,000, which is a little bit larger than what you typically see at pre-seed, meaning that we're going to have a slightly more concentrated portfolio. So looking to have somewhere in the neighborhood of 24 to maybe 30 companies in total. And because we invest so early, we are industry agnostic. We don't do life sciences because, like, not the skill set. I don't know how to evaluate it therapeutic. I don't do just about anything else. But even though we go really early, we do look for two key things, right? So if it's a software tech-enabled company, we like to see a clearly repeatable or unique customer acquisition strategy. And if it's a physical product, we typically like physical products in consumer markets that have lacked innovation over the last decade or so, 10 years or plus. Because those two founders tend to be out-of-the-box thinkers and out-of-the-box problem solvers. And that's what we define as a rare breed entrepreneur.

[SPEAKER_01]
Well, that's a great overview, Mac. And I do want to get into the fundraise. But what really struck me about your fundraise in particular is that you decided to go down the 506C path where most managers go down the traditional 506B. But you didn't go down the rolling fund route. Tell us a little bit about what led to that decision.

[SPEAKER_00]
A lot of this just has to coincide with the fact that when I started soft-circling money and thinking about raising a fund was around the same time I started to become more active on Twitter. So from June to now, I've gone from 2,500 followers to 19,000. And within that, I saw a lot of value out of the community I was building on Twitter. And so AngelLess came out with their rolling fund and how the GPs could publicly disclose about their fundraise. And I thought that was really interesting. And that would allow me to harness the power that I've created on Twitter. But then when you start to dive into it, the way rolling funds do their LP returns, it's kind of, it's a little weird. There's a lot of intricacies to it. And what bothered me was a lot of my earliest LPs or earliest supporters were people who've been supporters of mine for like the last 10 years. They've seen my journey from a software developer to an entrepreneur to now being an investor and now wanting to be LPs. I wanted to make sure that they got the upside of every company I invested in, not a fund one, not just based off the sum amount of quarters they invested in. And so I decided, you know, not to do the rolling fund. But then I took a step back and I looked at it and I was like, why are rolling funds so cool? Because you can publicly solicit. It almost feels like a crowdfunding because you can just go to a website and click a button to subscribe. And then you get access to capital very quickly, right? You don't have these traditional closers. You get your access to the first quarter of money right away. And when I looked at it, none of those had to do with the actual rolling part. They were all kind of just technological and front facing. But all the issues that I had with it were structural. So I said, OK, let's remove the structural part and just do the front facing part. And so I said, well, you can just do that on the traditional front. And so me and my team kind of came together like, how would we set this up? And so we said, OK, well, if we want to be able to publish these goals, all of this is 506E. OK, bam. The downside on that is every investor must be an accredited investor. I don't have the option of having up to 35 unaccredited investors. And that means that every LP that comes into the fund has to go through a KYC process. Well, most funds do that anyway. That really wasn't that much of a downside. So we can do that. Having a website to come up and give people access to our docs. At first, we thought we were going to have to figure out a way to code it so people filled out a form. And then we would take the inputs and dynamically fill out a PDF file that people could then digitally sign. But luckily, Carta, who we use for our back office, they have a partnership with a product called Anduin. And so what Anduin does is they take subscription docs specifically and turn them into a guided signature process where all the fields are dynamic. That fit that part perfectly. And then the last piece was how do we get access to the capital right away? And that one was a little tricky. And so when we talked to Carta, they basically said, you know, we can't do it. We could do it so that whenever an LP signs up to put money in the fund, we could send them money right away. But it'd be easier for us to manage it if we just did a close every Friday. And we said, cool, we'll do weekly closes. So every week as a pool of LPs come in, we close those LPs that Friday and we can get access to that money right away, which gives us a little bit more flexibility and gives us access to it. And the way we handle this, we draw the money down into an escrow and then we pull the money from the escrow as we make investment, right? So that's kind of the way we set it up.

[SPEAKER_01]
Thanks, Mac, for sharing that. There's a lot to unbundle there. And I know a lot of the listeners here are considering raising a fund either using the rolling fund structure or at the very least thinking about 506C as a provision to allow them to publicly solicit. And we'll get into that during the show. But turning to you, Roy, for a minute, tell us a little bit about how you work with Fund One managers specifically and maybe take us back to when you met Mac.

[SPEAKER_02]
So first of all, I just want to say, if there are people out there who are looking to invest in funds as a way of, A, getting great LP returns, and B, learning about the startup ecosystem, which is where a lot of Fund One LPs do, hard to imagine you could do much better than backing Mac. And I'll dissect why I think that in a second, and we can talk about our experiences. And I'll use my view on that to explain how I see the ecosystem. So, you know, I was a founder. I would meet with VCs all the time, you know, raising money, whatever. And I had this feeling of like, man, these guys, like some of the stuff they do, I just don't understand why they do it. So maybe I just don't get it. And some of it is like, hmm, maybe they suck at their jobs. And, you know, one example of that is a lot of them were very closed about information in ways that just seemed harmful to them. So, for example, like you'd beg to get a meeting with somebody, go get in your car and drive down the 280 or the 101 and go to Sand Hill Road, sit there. And in 30 seconds, you'd be like, oh, my gosh, this person took this meeting because they felt obligated. And we're a complete mismatch for the strategy of their fund. I was like, why didn't it just make it easy for me to look at a website and see that? And so when we started Bloomberg Beta, part of our idea was let's just try to do things the way that we as founders would wish they had been done. And, you know, a lot of funds then were saying, oh, like serve the founder as the customer. But like then you actually talk to them and the GP would be like, yeah, sorry, I can't talk. I'm in Bali. And it's like, OK, doesn't sound sounds like marketing to me. And we're like, what if we treated it as more than marketing? We were just religious about it. And transparency was a big part of that, because I think transparency, while it's very time consuming and takes effort and you expose risk. Like I remember before we published our first version of our website, which is, as you know, I think, you know, is what was once upon a time the internal operating manual for a fund. And it's just redirected to a GitHub repository. You know, we had people on our team being like, wait, hold on. We're going to disclose the average valuation. Like what? Like that could hurt us in negotiations. Then, you know, the risks were real risks. And so we went out to go do it. And I think what this reflects is a mentality that and this will zero into how we think about fund ones that, you know what? Starting a fund, it's actually no different than starting any other business on one level, which is you're starting a company that's competitive. It has a product. Its product is investments. You know, you can choose who you see as your customer. There are definitely some firms that choose to see the LP as their customer. However, we choose to see our LP as a supplier of capital and a business partner. And obviously, there are many groups internally at Bloomberg who we could talk to about technology trends. And we have, therefore, a client-like relationship with them. But our customer is founders. Like our primary customer is founders. And when you start thinking that way, you realize, okay, well, why are VC funds set up in the way they are? And a lot of it has to do with the regulatory history. Like why are VC funds so closed off? A lot of it is because private equity funds were very closed off. And so they just adopted the habit. And when we see fund ones, what we see is businesses that create a super normal return because fund ones tend to outperform. You probably know the data on that, Samir, much better than I do. And then it's like, well, okay, well, why aren't more people backing fund ones? And part of it is they're just not equipped to assess them because what do you have in a fund one? You're effectively, for almost all funds, you're backing somebody's taste. And it's like, okay, well, how well do I need to know somebody to back their taste? And, you know, Mac was describing some of these people he's had along the way with him in relationships, like longstanding working relationships. So, of course, those people are in a position to back his taste because they know him and they trust him and they have a feel for it. And, by the way, very parallel to the friends and family round for an early stage company where it's like, okay, you're betting on the founder. Well, who's best position to assess the founder? Not some professional founder assessor who's going to sit there and look into the person's eyes and be like, I just know. You know, I remember I think somebody affiliated with YC once said, like, I just meet a founder and I just know. Like, that sounds terrifying to me because I think what we know about human judgment is, A, that introduces lots of biases. And, you know, by the way, enter racism, sexism, like, you know, all kinds of biases. Come on, we can't possibly be that good at that. And so what we said for Bloomberg Beta is, wait a minute, maybe there's a chance for some super normal return here for us as an investor. If we said there are startups out there and those startups happen to have the business model of venture capital fund. But if we can invest in them in a way that makes sense for us, maybe we can produce super normal returns. So then, you know, we started like looking seriously at doing that. And we realized two things. One is investing in a fund is actually not the same as investing in a company in the sense that you're just investing in one product that they will have for a few years. That company, the firm, will exist like the distinction between a fund and a firm. That firm will exist for a very long time. And we, as long term backers and founders, we wrote a few LP checks. And then like two years later, like, OK, what about fund two? And I'm like, wait a minute. Hold on. Like, OK, I guess that's a little like a follow on financing. Sure. Maybe we'll do it. Fund three. It's like we don't have enough money to keep growing with you. And then the relationship does kind of not end, but it but you no longer have an active business relationship with them in quite the same way. And so we learned about this practice of seeding, which I'm sure many of your listeners know about. That is mostly something from the hedge fund world, which is confusingly. It's called seeding in our world where we also have seed investments where people invest in the firm. And an early LP might also invest in the GP or the management company. It's structured in different ways at different times. And the advantage of that is it creates long term alignment. We're like, oh, no, I want to make money when you make money over your whole journey, however long that lasts. And we can get into, you know, the pros and cons of it. And, you know, there's just lots of it's new adventure, relatively new. Although my understanding is that Sequoia was seeded in this way. There may be some other major firms that were seeded in this way. I don't want to name names because if I picked it up privately, it's not my information to share. And we wanted to explore doing that. And so that's how we think about fund ones is we're looking. We do them very rarely, maybe at the clip of like one or two a year. The single biggest issue we run into is and this is something that we talked Mac a bunch about is, OK, now we're investing in your firm. What determines the value of our investment? Well, returns are a big part of it, but actually AUM is the single factor that matters more than any other. And the people who seed hedge funds, when I started talking to them about why don't you do venture, they're like, oh, because the AUM doesn't rise fast enough. If you're like a great seed investor, your fund two is like 15. Your fund three is 40. I'm not making up numbers, you know, something like that. And, you know, they're in the world where it's like you have great returns for 18 months. You could have a billion dollars under management. So it's just a totally different world. And that's what one thing we're just trying to work through right now. We have invested in seeding arrangements where there is some different strategy that could drive very rapid AUM growth. And the last thing I'll say about it and shut up is I would not seed my own fund, my own firm. And the reason is many VCs. I think this is a valid choice are actually not solving for the economic value of the GP of their stake or their firm. They're solving for highest returns for LPs and they're solving for playing the role they want to play in the startup ecosystem. Like I like serving very early stage founders. We are day zero investors. We write a half a million to a million dollar check for 10% of a company. It's what we've been doing consistently for years. Future of work has been our focus from day one of our fund. I like that. Is it the thing that makes me the most money I could possibly make? No, it is not. You know, if we wanted to make more money, we'd try to have bigger funds. We'd try to do a lot of other things, but it's the work that I like doing. And I kind of think of it as craftsman work or craftsperson work. It's sort of like, you know, my dad was an architect. Did he try to make the most money he possibly could? No, he liked practicing architecture and he did well, you know, enough, you know, certainly to like provide for our family and, you know, all kinds of things. My mom also did work. And so we were we were able to have a stable living. You know, he did it out of a practice of the craft. And I think a lot of VCs are like that. So that's a very long winded rant on us and how we do fund ones. But it sort of puts in context how we see it. I'd just say if I had one hundred million dollars and somebody said, what's the best way to deploy this right now? I'd say go start a fund of funds for fund ones. I'd call it first. Yes, capital. If anybody else already said yes to you, it'd be too late for us. And we would just go out and write meaningful LP checks and see them, which out of our seventy five million dollar vehicle is a struggle.

[SPEAKER_01]
I mean, there's a lot of great insight and there's a lot to unpack there. You're right in saying that in the hedge fund world, we've seen seeding as a typical practice, very rarely in venture. Although we have seen more venture funds strategically invest in fund ones and fund twos as a way to generate deal flow. But that leads me to the general fundraising world. And we've seen this massive increase in the number of fund ones over the last few years. And Mac, you're going through this right now. Tell us a little bit about how the fundraise is going. You've raised money as an entrepreneur in the past. How is this different?

[SPEAKER_00]
It's really not much different for me because the first time I raised funding as an entrepreneur, I didn't know what the hell I was doing. I had a limited network and I was just trying to figure my way through it. Right. And somehow along the way, I figured it out. Well, I'm finding out as a GP starting my own fund, like experiencing the same thing. Right. Like I've never had to raise money for a fund. And my personal network of people who could be LPs was limited. So I kind of had to fumble my way through and figure it out. Right. Like Twitter was a gigantic help and a really big boost for me that it allowed me. It was a combination of things. Right. I was growing an audience in Twitter at the same time where everybody was in the house because of the pandemic around us. And so I was able to have meetings with people in very rapid succession in a very short amount of time. You know, I told people from the time of from June to September, I had over eleven hundred meetings. It's really close to twelve hundred meetings. Right. That's doing like 20 to 24 meetings a day.

[SPEAKER_02]
So one of the reasons I think that you are such a great bet for somebody who cares about LP returns is I talk to other fund one managers and I see the things that are distinctive. One of them is a lot of people have big Twitter presences that they built sort of doing something else and they want to convert that into being a fund manager. It's obviously not enough. You said intentionally, I'm going to go out and try to do this. It's a strategy. And then, man, like you just made it look easy getting to that followership and you're still growing. And I'm sure it wasn't. I'm sure it was intentional. And by the way, side note, we'd love to unpack how you thought about offering value to the community to do that. But the thing I'm curious about, the other thing is you sound and maybe this is because you did so many meetings in a lot of ways, like an LP where like you can describe allocation and strategy and think in terms of how the capital seeking returns things. If you had to score now where you are in terms of like, imagine another Mac, somebody like you going out and raising or the typical first time GP. What are the things where you're like, OK, now I now that I've done twelve hundred meetings, which that is fucking crazy. Pardon my French. Like I heard Charles Hudson once told me he did three hundred LP meetings and I was like, oh, my God, that's nuts. And he's like, no, no, no, actually, that's typical. Maybe a little much, but typical. And this is crazy. It's blown my mind. What do you feel like you've figured out versus what do you still feel like you're trying to figure out compared to other kind of fund one GPs?

[SPEAKER_00]
I've figured out my voice and what my brand is and what the value of that is. I'm still learning the fundraising process, though, right? Like, so I figured out what's unique and I think I was unique about me compared to other first time GPs and other GPs in general. And I figured out how to leverage that and speaking to potential LBs. I've also figured out that there's so many people out here in this world that are considered accredited investors that most people don't think of. I will say within our LP base, there's a good 10 or 15 folks where we would be their first ever LP check. We're the first exposure they've ever had. But to your point, I now also have a community of emerging GPs who are following me and who I'm part of. And I can tell the difference, right? I can tell, like, when the emerging GP is just getting started or when they haven't really thought through their portfolio construction or when they have. I guess the biggest thing is just, like, really understanding what works well for me, especially when it comes to pitching, right? So, like, I had a conversation earlier today where I was part of a panel where it was really a group of us pitching to a group of LPs. And as part of that, my two counterparts used decks. And they asked us, if you have a presentation, send it to us. I didn't send a presentation because I've never actually pitched anybody with a deck. And so I was going to stick with what works well for me. And one thing, and this is a piece of advice I'll give the GPs who are listening, is that while I was raising, one of the things that I do and I do well naturally is I'm a naturally good storyteller. Storytelling is what I do. And what I found was being able to tell a story of a company that I've supported and that I worked with and about the funding journey is not only impactful, but it's something that apparently not enough GPs actually do when they're fundraising. They kind of throw up their deck and kind of just go through the motions and talk through all the numbers and the structure. Like, yeah, everybody has very similar numbers and structures and little tweaks here and there. But what really makes you different as a GP? I've been able to figure out how to get that out when I talk to people.

[SPEAKER_01]
You know, it's really interesting that you bring that up. And I've said this before publicly, that storytelling is such a big part of being a VC. Because what people are really looking at is, can you compel entrepreneurs to want to work with you? And are you offering something that is clearly articulated in what you add as a VC from a value-add perspective? It's funny that you bring up 1,100 meetings, which is just absolutely incredible in such short amount of time. And I had both Charles Hudson and actually Elizabeth Yin on the podcast before. And Elizabeth actually mentioned 700 LPs. And I remember in my Twitter mentions, everyone's like, oh my God, 700 different LP. How did you actually do that? Part of this is like logistically, you can do more meetings right now, given that we're in a Zoom environment. But I suspect that you get a lot of feedback. And if you're having 24 meetings a day, your head can spin on what feedback do you take? How do you refine your pitch? Were there times during the whole thing where you're just saying, you know, the LP feedback that I'm getting, one is probably all over the place. Some people are saying X, some people are saying Y. How do you distill that down into refining and improving your pitch and thesis?

[SPEAKER_00]
The benefit I have going through this process is I've gone through the same thing as a founder, right? Like as a founder, if you ever go through an accelerator, like the last month of the accelerator is nothing but pitch practice, right? And every day you're getting feedback from some different person telling you how you need to change your pitch or what you need to do different. And over time, you just find the notes within the pitch that resonate. And you just realize it's not going to resonate with everybody. So you try to hit the things that resonate with the majority of people and stick with that. When I talk about, you know, my fundraising, when I tell my story, I talk about that I had two startups. One had an exit and one failed. You know, I've had people tell me, don't talk about the failure. You know, people don't like someone who's gone through a failure. But for me, it's just part of my story. It's part of my authenticity, right? The fact that I failed, I learned a lot. And it helps me also better evaluate entrepreneurs. Because I know the arrogance I felt when I failed. And I know the things that I didn't look out for because I just knew everything, right? I can now see that and found it, right? I also know the humbleness I have when I succeeded and all the things that I did wrong and how I was able to work through those. And so even though I have gotten the feedback that don't talk about your failures, nobody wants to hear about a failure, I don't view it that way. I talk about it, for me, it's unlearning, right? And so if you're an LP and you don't consider that, that's okay. You know, I might not be the right, you know, investment for you. Granted, I'm probably the right investment for any LP because I'm a return to capital. But that's just in my estimation.

[SPEAKER_02]
When you say that, I hear, as you're taking a note, I hear the it's a search, not a sell process. And you said you're kind of going to the thing that works for the majority of LPs. I kind of wish we lived in a world where you could say it the way you wish to say it and live with the subset of LPs for whom it is actually a match. And I think one of the challenges here is that the current world of Fund One fundraising, and maybe to some broader extent, LP fundraising. I mean, look, let's be honest. We have one LP. I've written more LP checks than I have taken LP pitch meetings to pitch anything out. So I know one side of this and not the other. So who knows? But I talk to a lot of LPs. They often call me to get references on founders because they know I'm not going to be pitching them. But I think a thing that happens is there is so much scarcity or perceived scarcity of how many LPs there are who are willing to support you that you kind of can't just be like, well, I'll just shrug it off and find the people I find. And I don't know, I guess I'm just raising the question of how true is that, you know, you are breaking new people into being LPs who have never been LPs before. I think that actually happens with almost every Fund One I've ever seen. And that's both good in the sense you're drawing people in and weird and bad in the sense it's a sign that there's a gap in the market. It's one of the reasons I just say I'm really into this idea of like YC for VCs kind of model that, you know, AngelList has done some stuff. If operator has done some stuff, recast a bunch of folks out there who have been doing this kind of like multi, Samir, the media you do is an example of this. Open LP is an example of this. But I'm curious, Mac, to what extent, you know, maybe it raises another question. And actually, I asked both of you because I'm just curious to what extent you guys feel like a Fund One founder can say, you know what? I'm just going to do things my way and search for the people who are a match versus do they feel prey to the fact that there's just scarce dollars out there willing to write LP checks?

[SPEAKER_01]
Roy, I'll take a crack at that question. And I do think that there's a perception that capital is much more scarce than it is. There's a lot of liquidity sloshing around right now within the non-institutional market. There's 200,000 ultra high net worth individuals that have investable assets over $50 million. There's 11,000 global family offices. And given the yield environment right now, people are desperate to find places to place capital and earn alpha type of returns. The challenge, though, for a GP is discovering these people and being discovered. And because of that, what ends up happening is GPs are forced to go down the path of telling a story that is most likely to resonate with the masses versus, you know, having highly relevant conversations with those that are going to be the best fit. But, Mac, you know, curiously, from your perspective, when you talk to all of these LPs, and you mentioned this earlier, there's a subsection that is very much, hey, I'm learning venture first time. But for the ones that have invested in venture before, what are the type of questions that you've been asked consistently? And even maybe going back to when you talked to Roy, what are the pressure points that every single fund one manager should know that is going to be asked during that fundraise?

[SPEAKER_00]
I mean, everybody wants to know about your portfolio construction and why you've set it the way you have. I consistently get the question of, are you sure you want to do just that few investments? You know, a pre-see, you probably should be doing more. I get that a lot. I get the question a lot around deal sourcing. How do I handle my deal sourcing or where do I get my sources? How do I handle the abundance of inbound that I get because my Twitter presence is so strong? And I'm very much cold intros. You can just directly email me. There's a caveat to that, though. I tell founders, like, just because I take cold intros doesn't mean I'm going to read every single one. Like, you know, if I get 100 intros in a day, I'm going to read like 10 of them. So just keep that in mind. Like, yes, you can email me. There's a chance I'm going to read it. I'm not going to get to every single one if I'm inundated, right? So, like, there is some give and take there. And I think founders get confused when we talk about cold intros or being able to say that we read cold intros. So I get pressed on that.
